title: Computer Vision
text:
Preface
These notes follow CS 585, Image and Video Computing, as taught by Margrit Betke at Boston University in Spring 2024, using the lecture schedule and readings on the course’s schedule page. The first chapter covers the block on programming with images, where we follow three sets of lecture notes closely. Lecture notes 1 is a short deck on the pitfalls of programming with images, by Diane Theriault and Margrit Betke (Lecture notes 1), Lecture notes 2 is the January 30 lecture on skin colour, image differencing, template matching and image pyramids (Lecture notes 2), and Lecture notes 3 is a case study of the KidsRoom, an interactive story space built at the MIT Media Lab by Aaron Bobick and colleagues, which watched children play using little more than subtracted video frames (Lecture notes 3). The later chapters follow the rest of the schedule, image formation, tracking, edges and optical flow, deep learning and faces, stereo and multiple views, and finally generative models, reflectance, registration, transformers and ethics, built around the topics and readings listed for each lecture together with the standard papers and textbooks, mainly Horn’s Robot Vision (MIT Press, 1986) and Szeliski’s Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications.
The slides are pretty terse (as slides should be), and a lot of the real content was said out loud or written on the board, so a student reading the PDFs a week later is basically left to reconstruct it on their own. So what I’m trying to do here is fill in that missing layer, which means that wherever a slide states a formula we derive it, and wherever a slide names an algorithm we write it out in Python and run it on a small example you can check by hand.
I’m assuming you can program, and that you remember a little bit of calculus and linear algebra, but not that you’ve ever opened an image file in code before. Everything is done with three libraries, NumPy for arrays, OpenCV for reading files (and a few other conveniences), and Matplotlib for looking at the results, so if you’re starting from scratch, this is all you need.
pip install numpy opencv-python matplotlib
A quick word on how to read these notes. Chapter 1 is about what an image actually is inside a computer, binary images and the shapes in them, finding faces and finding motion, and it has most of the traps people fall into in their first week, so if you only read one chapter carefully, make it that one. Chapter 2 asks where the numbers in an image come from, with pinhole cameras, vanishing points, lenses and a first look at stereo. Chapter 3 is about change, following objects with the alpha-beta and Kalman filters, associating detections with tracks, finding edges and active contours, and measuring optical flow. Chapter 4 brings in deep learning and faces and then the geometry of two and more views, and Chapter 5 covers the rest of the course, from GANs and diffusion models to photometric stereo, registration, transformers and the ethics of all of this.
One last remark. A lot of the methods here are old (some of them are from the 1970s), and most modern systems would just hand these jobs to a neural network, which is fine, but these are the ideas that the networks are quietly rediscovering anyway, and they’re also the tools you end up reaching for at two in the morning when you need something that works on a webcam and you don’t have any training data at all.






NoteRunning the code in these notes



Every Python cell in this book was run when the page was built, so the output is already there to read. Each cell also has a Run button. The first time you press one, the page downloads Python together with NumPy, OpenCV and Matplotlib (about 35 MB, which your browser then keeps) and runs the code right in the page. Nothing needs installing. A few cells in the later chapters also use SciPy, which the page fetches the first time one of them runs. You can edit any cell and run it again, and your output replaces the printed one.
Python in the browser is slower than on a laptop, and some packages, PyTorch among them, are not available there. For those, run the code on your own computer instead. Download start_kernel.py and requirements.txt from the course page, install the packages with pip install -r requirements.txt, and run python start_kernel.py. It opens this book connected to Python on your machine.

title: 1  Programming with Images
text:
1.1 Images Are Grids of Numbers
The first thing to get used to is almost embarrassingly simple, which is that to a program a picture is just a rectangular array of integers (and really nothing more than that). Every hard problem in computer vision lives somewhere in the gap between that array and the things we actually see in it, like a face or a tumor, but before we start worrying about that gap we should be completely at home with the array itself, because a surprising number of bugs in vision code turn out to have basically nothing to do with vision.
Setup: create the test files used in this chapter
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. This cell creates the small test files that the code
# below expects to find: face.jpg (a synthetic scene with a skin-coloured face and a wooden door),
# picture.raw (a 512 x 512 grey image stored as raw bytes) and clip.avi (a short video of a
# dark square sliding across a noisy background). Run it once before anything else.
import numpy as np
import cv2

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# face.jpg
scene = np.full((240, 320, 3), (90, 100, 95), np.uint8)
scene = np.clip(scene + rng.normal(0, 6, scene.shape), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
face_mask = np.zeros((240, 320), np.uint8)
cv2.ellipse(face_mask, (200, 120), (35, 48), 0, 0, 360, 1, -1)
shade = np.linspace(0.6, 1.1, 320)[None, :, None]          # uneven lighting, left to right
skin = np.clip(np.array([120, 150, 200], float) * shade + rng.normal(0, 5, scene.shape), 0, 255)
scene[face_mask == 1] = skin[face_mask == 1].astype(np.uint8)
scene[30:200, 20:70] = (60, 110, 165)                       # a wooden door
cv2.imwrite("face.jpg", scene, [cv2.IMWRITE_JPEG_QUALITY, 95])

# picture.raw
pic = np.full((512, 512), 200, np.uint8)
pic[:, 100:140] = 30          # a dark vertical bar starting at column 100
pic[300:320, :] = 90          # a grey horizontal bar
pic.tofile("picture.raw")

# clip.avi
bg = cv2.GaussianBlur(rng.uniform(120, 220, (120, 160)), (0, 0), 3)
writer = cv2.VideoWriter("clip.avi", cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*"MJPG"), 30, (160, 120))
for t in range(30):
    f = bg.copy()
    f[50:80, 10 + 3 * t : 40 + 3 * t] = 40                  # moves 3 pixels per frame
    f = np.clip(f + rng.normal(0, 3, f.shape), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
    writer.write(cv2.cvtColor(f, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2BGR))
writer.release()
print("created face.jpg, picture.raw and clip.avi")


created face.jpg, picture.raw and clip.avi

TipExercises



Programming exercises show up at the end of the subsections they practise, and they’re numbered by subsection. Each one has a cell for your code, which starts out as a function whose body just raises NotImplementedError, followed by a check cell. Press Edit on the exercise cell, replace the raise line with your own code, press Run, and then run the check below it. The checks print what they find and never stop the page, so Run all works whether or not you’ve done any of the exercises yet.



1.1.1 From light to numbers
Picture the image plane inside a camera. Light lands on it, and at each point (x, y) there’s some brightness, which we’ll call E(x, y). This is a function of two continuous variables that also takes continuous values, and a computer can store neither of those things, so the camera ends up doing two things to it.
First it samples. The sensor is a grid of small light-sensitive cells, and each cell reports the light averaged over its own little patch, so the continuous plane turns into a grid with M rows and N columns, and each cell of that grid is a pixel (short for picture element).
Then it quantizes. The value each cell reports gets rounded to one of a finite number of levels, and almost always there are 256 levels, the integers 0 through 255, because that’s exactly what fits in one byte (zero means black and 255 means white). Szeliski goes through both steps, along with the many ways real sensors fall short of this tidy picture, in Sections 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 of his book (Szeliski, 2nd ed., 2022).
It’s worth pausing for a second on how much information quantization actually throws away, because the answer is reassuringly little. Suppose brightness runs from 0 to 1 and we use L equally spaced levels, so the spacing is Δ = 1/(L − 1). Rounding to the nearest level makes an error e that sits somewhere between −Δ/2 and Δ/2, and if the true brightness isn’t somehow conspiring against us, e is equally likely to be anywhere in that interval, so its mean squared size is
\[
\langle e^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} e^2 \, de = \frac{1}{\Delta}\left[\frac{e^3}{3}\right]_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} = \frac{\Delta^2}{12}.
\]
With L = 256 the root mean square error is Δ/√12, which comes out to about 0.0011, so roughly a tenth of a percent of the full range. Our eyes can’t see that, and camera noise is usually bigger anyway, so eight bits per pixel isn’t really a crude approximation at all (which is probably why the format has lasted as long as it has).
A colour image just repeats the whole construction three times, once each for red, green and blue light, so each pixel holds three bytes instead of one.
Files on disk add one more layer on top of this. A JPEG throws away detail the eye probably won’t miss so that the file comes out small, while a PNG compresses without losing anything, and you’ll run into both. For our purposes the important point is that once a file is loaded the format is forgotten and we’re just left with the array. If you’re ever measuring something delicate, like the tiny brightness changes between two video frames, it’s better to use lossless files, since JPEG’s compression leaves faint blocky artifacts of its own that can look a lot like real signal.

Exercise 1.1.1 (Quantization error by experiment) We showed that rounding to L equally spaced levels between 0 and 1 leaves a root mean square error of Δ/√12, where Δ = 1/(L − 1), so let’s actually test that claim. Write quantize(signal, L), which rounds every value of an array in [0, 1] to the nearest of the levels 0, Δ, 2Δ and so on up to 1. The check runs it on a long, finely spaced ramp and compares the measured error with the formula for several values of L.


def quantize(signal, L):
    """Round each value of signal (all in [0, 1]) to the nearest of L equally spaced levels."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    ramp = np.linspace(0, 1, 200_001)
    ok = True
    for L in [4, 16, 64, 256]:
        q = quantize(ramp, L)
        delta = 1 / (L - 1)
        on_levels = np.allclose(q / delta, np.round(q / delta))
        rms = np.sqrt(np.mean((ramp - q) ** 2))
        predicted = delta / np.sqrt(12)
        print(f"L = {L:3d}   measured RMS {rms:.6f}   predicted {predicted:.6f}")
        ok = ok and on_levels and abs(rms / predicted - 1) < 0.01
    return ok

check("Exercise 1.1.1", test)

1.1.2 Opening an image
Here’s how we load an image in Python and look at what we get back. OpenCV gets imported under the name cv2, for historical reasons that nobody really remembers fondly.

import cv2
import numpy as np

img = cv2.imread("face.jpg")   # put the name of any image file here

print(type(img))    # <class 'numpy.ndarray'>
print(img.shape)    # e.g. (480, 640, 3): rows, columns, colour channels
print(img.dtype)    # uint8: unsigned 8-bit integers, 0 to 255
print(img[100, 200])  # the three numbers stored at row 100, column 200

<class 'numpy.ndarray'>
(240, 320, 3)
uint8
[112 141 185]


And that’s pretty much the whole story, the image is a NumPy array of shape (rows, columns, 3) whose entries are bytes.
There’s already one trap here though. If the file name is wrong, cv2.imread doesn’t raise an error, it prints a warning and quietly returns None (this behaviour is described in the OpenCV documentation for the image codecs module, OpenCV, imgcodecs), and then the program crashes several lines later with a confusing message about NoneType. So it’s a good habit to check right away.

img = cv2.imread("face.jpg")
if img is None:
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not read face.jpg. Check the path.")

We don’t always need a file, actually. Since an image is just an array we can build one by hand, and for testing algorithms that’s often the best thing to do, because then we know exactly what the right answer is supposed to be.

# A 4 x 6 black image with a small red square in it.
img = np.zeros((4, 6, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
img[1:3, 2:4] = (0, 0, 255)     # why (0, 0, 255) means red is explained in 1.1.4

cv2.imwrite("tiny.png", img)     # save it
back = cv2.imread("tiny.png")    # and read it back
print(np.array_equal(img, back)) # True, because PNG is lossless

True


To look at an image we’ll use Matplotlib, which plays nicely with notebooks.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rgb = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)   # again, see 1.1.4
plt.imshow(rgb)
plt.axis("off")
plt.show()










1.1.3 Rows, columns, x and y
Now for the trap that catches everyone at least once. Mathematicians write points as (x, y), with x going right and y going up, but arrays are indexed as img[row, col], with the row counting down from the top. So the pixel at horizontal position x and vertical position y is


Setup: choose a pixel
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. Choose a pixel of the tiny image to look at.
x, y = 3, 1



value = img[y, x]      # row first, then column

and the origin is the top-left corner, with y increasing downward. The shape of an image is likewise (height, width), which is the opposite of the “640 by 480” way we usually describe screens. And to make matters a bit worse, a lot of OpenCV’s drawing functions take points as (x, y), so when we draw a circle at the pixel we found with img[y, x], we pass (x, y).

h, w = img.shape[:2]                     # height first
cv2.circle(img, (x, y), 5, (0, 255, 0))  # but drawing wants (x, y)

There’s also a quieter consequence of this that’ll matter in Section 1.2. With y pointing down, our coordinate system is a mirror image of the one in textbooks, so an angle that’s measured counter-clockwise on paper comes out clockwise on the screen. Horn’s derivations in Robot Vision use the textbook convention, so when we turn his formula for an object’s orientation into code we have to remember which way our y axis points (it’s basically a sign error waiting to happen, and we’ll point it out again when we get there).

Exercise 1.1.2 (Rows, columns, x and y) Write mark_pixel(img, x, y, colour), which paints the pixel at horizontal position x and vertical position y in the BGR colour colour, along with its neighbours directly above, below, left and right. Neighbours that fall outside the image should just be skipped quietly. The function should change img in place and also return it. The check marks a pixel on a small black canvas and compares every entry of the array with what it should be, so a swapped x and y won’t slip through.


def mark_pixel(img, x, y, colour):
    """Paint pixel (x, y) and its four neighbours in the given BGR colour."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    canvas = np.zeros((6, 8, 3), np.uint8)
    mark_pixel(canvas, 5, 2, (0, 255, 0))
    expected = np.zeros((6, 8, 3), np.uint8)
    for row, col in [(2, 5), (1, 5), (3, 5), (2, 4), (2, 6)]:
        expected[row, col] = (0, 255, 0)
    corner = np.zeros((6, 8, 3), np.uint8)
    mark_pixel(corner, 0, 0, (255, 0, 0))          # two neighbours fall off the image
    corner_ok = corner[:, :, 0].sum() == 3 * 255 and corner[0, 0, 0] == 255
    if not np.array_equal(canvas, expected):
        print("pixels painted (row, col):", [tuple(int(v) for v in p) for p in np.argwhere(canvas.any(axis=2))])
    return np.array_equal(canvas, expected) and corner_ok

check("Exercise 1.1.2", test)

1.1.4 Colour and grey
The third index of a colour image picks the channel. You’d probably guess the order is red, green, blue, but in OpenCV it’s actually blue, green, red. The default loading flag is literally named IMREAD_COLOR_BGR in the documentation (OpenCV, imgcodecs), and it’s a leftover from back when BGR was a common ordering in camera drivers and Windows bitmap files (and nobody has dared change it since). That’s why the red square above was written as (0, 0, 255). Matplotlib, and pretty much every other library, expects red first, so if you show an OpenCV image in Matplotlib without converting it, faces turn blue and the sky turns orange.
A lot of algorithms want a single number per pixel, a greyscale image. The simplest choice is the plain average, and the course slides use exactly that when describing a segmentation pipeline (Betke, Segmentation lecture, slide 4).
\[
I = \frac{R + G + B}{3}
\]
OpenCV uses a weighted average instead, which its documentation gives as (OpenCV, colour conversions)
\[
Y = 0.299\,R + 0.587\,G + 0.114\,B .
\]
The weights come from television engineering. Our eyes are a lot more sensitive to green light than to blue, so a pure green patch looks much brighter to us than a pure blue patch of the same physical strength, and the weighted sum is trying to match perceived brightness. For most of what follows the choice barely matters, but it’s good to keep in mind that “grey” is a convention (it’s something people agreed on, the physics doesn’t hand it to us).

gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)   # uses the weighted formula

# The same thing by hand, to see there is no magic. Note the BGR order.
b = img[:, :, 0].astype(float)
g = img[:, :, 1].astype(float)
r = img[:, :, 2].astype(float)
mine = np.round(0.299 * r + 0.587 * g + 0.114 * b).astype(np.uint8)

On our tiny test image both of them give 76 inside the red square, which is just 0.299 × 255 rounded.

Exercise 1.1.3 (Two kinds of grey) Write gray_average(img), which returns the plain average (R + G + B)/3 of a BGR image as a uint8 image, rounded to the nearest whole number. The overflow trap of Section 1.1.5 is sitting there waiting for anyone who adds the three channels as they come. The check compares your result with OpenCV’s weighted grey on face.jpg and reports where the two disagree the most, so look at the colour of that pixel and think about why the disagreement is largest there. As a warm-up, convince yourself that img[:, :, ::-1], which reverses the order of the channel axis, is the same array as cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB) (the check tests that too).


def gray_average(img):
    """(R + G + B) / 3 of a BGR uint8 image, rounded, as a uint8 image."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    scene = cv2.imread("face.jpg")
    mine = gray_average(scene)
    reference = np.round(scene.astype(float).mean(axis=2)).astype(np.uint8)
    flip_ok = np.array_equal(scene[:, :, ::-1], cv2.cvtColor(scene, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB))
    print("img[:, :, ::-1] equals the BGR to RGB conversion:", flip_ok)
    gap = np.abs(mine.astype(int) - cv2.cvtColor(scene, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY).astype(int))
    r, c = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(gap), gap.shape)
    print(f"largest disagreement {gap.max()} grey levels, at row {r}, column {c}, where (B, G, R) = {tuple(int(v) for v in scene[r, c])}")
    return mine.dtype == np.uint8 and np.array_equal(mine, reference)

check("Exercise 1.1.3", test)

1.1.5 Arithmetic that bites
Here’s probably the most important pitfall in this whole section. The entries of an image are of type uint8, unsigned 8-bit integers, and when arithmetic on them goes outside the range 0 to 255, NumPy doesn’t complain and doesn’t clip either, it just wraps around, keeping only the remainder after division by 256. The NumPy documentation actually warns about this in its section on overflow errors for fixed-size types (NumPy, Data types).

a = np.array([200, 50], dtype=np.uint8)
b = np.array([100, 100], dtype=np.uint8)

print(a + b)   # [ 44 150]   because 300 - 256 = 44
print(a - b)   # [100 206]   because -50 + 256 = 206

[ 44 150]
[100 206]


Read that second line again, because subtracting a brighter pixel from a darker one gives a large positive number. In Section 1.4 we’ll subtract one video frame from the next to find motion, and if we forget about this, every dark object moving across a bright background produces complete nonsense. The cure is to convert to a wider type before doing any arithmetic, and only convert back at the end (if at all).

print(a.astype(int) + b)   # [300 150]
print(a.astype(int) - b)   # [100 -50]

[300 150]
[100 -50]


We’ll do this every single time. It costs a little memory and saves a whole lot of confusion.
The second pitfall is a bit subtler. Slicing a NumPy array doesn’t copy it, it gives you a view into the same memory, so writing into the slice writes into the original image.

big = np.zeros((5, 5), dtype=np.uint8)
crop = big[1:3, 1:3]
crop[:] = 255          # this also changes big!

safe = big[1:3, 1:3].copy()   # an independent copy

Sometimes that’s exactly what we want, and sometimes it’s the reason a template we cut from the first video frame keeps changing as we draw on later frames. OpenCV’s drawing functions also change the image you hand them in place, so if you want to keep the original around, draw on a copy.
The last pitfall is about display. When Matplotlib is handed a single-channel image it doesn’t show it in grey by default, and on top of that it rescales the values so that the darkest pixel is black and the brightest is white, so an almost uniform image ends up looking like it has dramatic contrast. To see what’s really there, you have to say so explicitly.

plt.imshow(gray, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255)









Exercise 1.1.4 (Brightening without wrap-around) Write brighten(img, amount), which adds amount to every pixel of a uint8 image and returns a new uint8 image (the amount can be negative). Values should stop at 0 and 255 instead of wrapping around, and the image you were handed shouldn’t change. Once your function passes, the check shows face.jpg brightened by 100 the naive way, with img + 100, next to your version, and the naive one is worth a long look, because those garish patches are what wrap-around looks like in the wild.


def brighten(img, amount):
    """Add amount to every pixel, clipping to [0, 255]. Returns a new uint8 image."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    a = np.array([[0, 100, 250]], dtype=np.uint8)
    up, down = brighten(a, 10), brighten(a, -50)
    ok = (up.dtype == np.uint8 and up.tolist() == [[10, 110, 255]]
          and down.tolist() == [[0, 50, 200]] and a.tolist() == [[0, 100, 250]])
    if ok:
        scene = cv2.imread("face.jpg")
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
        axes[0].imshow(cv2.cvtColor(scene + 100, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)); axes[0].set_title("scene + 100 (wraps around)")
        axes[1].imshow(cv2.cvtColor(brighten(scene, 100), cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)); axes[1].set_title("brighten(scene, 100)")
        for ax in axes:
            ax.axis("off")
        plt.show()
    else:
        print("brighten([[0, 100, 250]], 10) gave", up.tolist(), "and with -50 gave", down.tolist())
    return ok

check("Exercise 1.1.4", test)

Exercise 1.1.4: not attempted yet




1.1.6 When the bytes are read wrong
Lecture notes 1 has a sentence that every vision programmer eventually learns the hard way, which is that when an image comes out looking strange, the path from the strange look back to the actual bug is often far from obvious (Lecture notes 1, slide 4). The deck then walks through a gallery of characteristic failures, and each one has a recognizable visual signature, so once you know the signatures you can pretty much diagnose the bug just from the picture. The deck also recommends two tools of the trade. One is OpenCV, which started out as an Intel project and has become the standard open-source vision library, and the other is IrfanView, a free image viewer that’s handy for flipping through thousands of saved video frames in a batch.
The colour-order mistake from Section 1.1.4 is the first entry in the gallery, with a portrait turned eerily blue (Lecture notes 1, slide 5). The others show up when we read pixel data ourselves rather than going through cv2.imread, which happens more often than you might think (camera drivers hand over raw buffers, and some scientific instruments write files with no header at all). All of that data is stored the same way, one row after another, and NumPy can read it directly.

W, H = 512, 512                                     # we must know these from somewhere
raw = np.fromfile("picture.raw", dtype=np.uint8)    # every byte in the file
print(raw.size, "bytes; expected", W * H)
img = raw.reshape(H, W)                             # cut the long line into rows

262144 bytes; expected 262144


The print line is honestly the most useful debugging tool in this subsection. If the byte count isn’t exactly width × height × channels, then one of those three numbers is wrong, and no amount of staring at the picture will get you there as quickly.
Wrong width. Suppose the true width is W but we reshape with a slightly smaller width W′ = W − δ. The slides show the case W = 512, W′ = 508 and get an image full of strong diagonal stripes (Lecture notes 1, slide 6), and we can actually predict exactly what those stripes look like. Because rows are stored one after another, the pixel in row r and column c lives at position k = rW + c in the file, and when we reshape with width W′ it gets displayed in row ⌊k/W′⌋ and column k mod W′. Now write
\[
k = rW + c = rW' + (r\delta + c).
\]
As long as rδ + c is still less than W′, this pixel lands in the same row r but in column c + rδ, so each row is displayed δ pixels further to the right than the row above it. A vertical edge at column c₀ therefore turns into a slanted line, moving δ pixels to the right for every row it goes down, and with δ = 4 that’s a shallow line about 14° below the horizontal (since arctan(1/4) ≈ 14°). Once the shift grows past the width, which happens after W′/δ = 127 rows, it wraps around and the pattern repeats, and that’s exactly the striped look on the slide. In our own test with a dark vertical bar at column 100, the wrongly reshaped image had the bar start at column 104 in row 1, 108 in row 2 and 140 in row 10.

wrong = raw[: (raw.size // 508) * 508].reshape(-1, 508)   # deliberately wrong width

Wrong colour depth. A grey image uses one byte per pixel and a colour image uses three, and if we mix them up the arithmetic goes wrong in an equally predictable way (Lecture notes 1, slide 7). Suppose a grey image gets read as if it were colour, with the right width W. Each displayed pixel then grabs three neighbouring grey values and treats them as blue, green and red. Neighbouring pixels are similar, so the result looks roughly grey, but the small differences between them show up as faint colour, and on smooth gradients the three channels drift in and out of step so that up close you see bands of rainbow. The geometry breaks too. A displayed row now eats up 3W bytes, which is three real rows, so its first third shows real row 3r′ squeezed horizontally by a factor of three, its middle third shows row 3r′ + 1, and its last third shows row 3r′ + 2, and the picture comes out as three narrow copies of itself side by side, only a third as tall. Read a colour image as grey and the opposite happens, the picture gets stretched and covered in fine vertical stripes.
Text mode versus binary mode. The last gotcha in the deck is the strangest-looking one (Lecture notes 1, slide 8). Files can be opened as text or as raw binary data, and in text mode the operating system tries to be helpful about line endings. Windows marks the end of a line with two bytes, a carriage return followed by a newline, and when a file is opened as text the carriage returns get quietly removed. (The slide writes the carriage return’s value as 20, but it’s byte 13 in decimal, or 0x0D in hexadecimal.) In an image, of course, 13 is just a rather dark grey value, and it turns up all over the place.
Every time a byte disappears, every byte after it shifts one place to the left. In a colour image this rotates the channels, so what should have been blue gets read as green and green as red, until the next lost byte rotates them again, and the picture breaks into horizontal bands of wrong colour, each one starting at a row where a 13 happened to occur. Python 3 does this translation in text mode on every operating system (not just Windows), and with its default text encoding it’ll usually crash with a decoding error before you even get that far. In our test, the bytes [10, 13, 10, 200, 13, 13, 10, 26, 5] came back from a text-mode read as [10, 10, 200, 10, 10, 26, 5]. The fix is a single letter.

with open("picture.raw", "rb") as f:      # the b means binary. Never leave it out.
    data = f.read()
img = np.frombuffer(data, dtype=np.uint8).reshape(H, W)

None of these traps is deep, but every one of them has cost students hours, and every one of them shows up again in the algorithms below. So now, with the array firmly in hand, we can start asking it questions.

Exercise 1.1.5 (The mystery file) The setup cell at the top of this chapter wrote a file called mystery.raw. It holds a grey image, one byte per pixel and no header, and nobody told us its width. Write guess_width(raw, candidates), which picks the width from a list of candidates. Here’s the idea. At the right width, each row sits directly above the row that really followed it, and in a natural picture neighbouring rows look alike, while at a wrong width the rows get sheared against each other, as we saw in Section 1.1.6. So try each candidate, reshape, and measure the average absolute difference between consecutive rows, and the smallest one wins. The check passes in every width that divides the file size exactly, and shows you the picture at the width you chose.


def guess_width(raw, candidates):
    """Return the candidate width that makes neighbouring rows of the image most alike."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    raw = np.fromfile("mystery.raw", dtype=np.uint8)
    candidates = [w for w in range(64, 2001) if raw.size % w == 0]
    print(len(candidates), "candidate widths, from", candidates[0], "to", candidates[-1])
    w = guess_width(raw, candidates)
    picture = raw.reshape(-1, w)
    plt.imshow(picture, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255)
    plt.title(f"mystery.raw at width {w}")
    plt.show()
    row_change = np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(picture.astype(int), axis=0)))
    print(f"average change between neighbouring rows at this width: {row_change:.2f} grey levels")
    return row_change < 3.5

check("Exercise 1.1.5", test)

1.2 Binary Images and the Shapes in Them
The simplest thing we can do with a grey image is to throw away almost everything in it. We decide, pixel by pixel, whether it belongs to the thing we care about or to the background, and we write down a 1 or a 0, and what’s left is a binary image. It sounds like a crude move (and it is), but it’s kind of remarkable how much can be measured from a binary image, and the measurements turn out to have a clean mathematical structure. Both lectures we follow lean on this material, and the course lists it as reading for this block, in the form of the Wikipedia article on image moments, notes on binary image analysis, a reading on thresholding and Horn’s Chapter 3. The slides that go with it come from the neighbouring lectures, the blackboard lecture on moments and the January 25 deck (Betke, Jan 25 2024, slides 2 to 13), with Chapter 3 of Horn’s Robot Vision as the main reference for the derivations.
Throughout, B(x, y) is the binary image, which equals 1 on the object and 0 everywhere else.

1.2.1 Thresholding
The standard way to get B from a grey image I is to pick a number τ, called the threshold, and compare every pixel against it. The slides write this as
\[
B(x,y) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } I(x,y) > \tau, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
\]
This marks bright things as the object, and when the object is dark on a light background (like the bat in the slides) we just flip the inequality. In code the whole operation is a single comparison, which NumPy applies to every pixel at once.


Setup: the test ellipse used in this section
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. The test image used throughout Section 1.2: a dark ellipse
# (grey value 60, semi-axes 80 and 25, tilted 30 degrees) on a background of 180, plus noise of
# standard deviation 10. img is a colour copy to draw on.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
gray = np.full((200, 300), 180, dtype=np.uint8)
cv2.ellipse(gray, (150, 100), (80, 25), 30, 0, 360, 60, -1)
gray = np.clip(gray.astype(float) + rng.normal(0, 10, gray.shape), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
img = cv2.cvtColor(gray, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2BGR)



def threshold(gray, tau):
    """Binary image that is 1 wherever the pixel is darker than tau."""
    return (gray < tau).astype(np.uint8)

B = threshold(gray, 120)

The interesting question is how to choose τ. The segmentation lecture lists several methods (Betke, Segmentation lecture, slides 5 to 10), and almost all of them start from the histogram, where H(g) counts how many pixels have grey value g, for each g from 0 to 255.

hist = np.bincount(gray.ravel(), minlength=256)   # hist[g] = number of pixels with value g

plt.bar(range(256), hist, width=1.0)
plt.xlabel("grey value"); plt.ylabel("number of pixels")
plt.show()








If the picture is a dark object on a light background, the histogram typically has two humps, one for the object and one for the background, with a valley in between, and every method below is basically a different way of finding that valley.
Absolute thresholding. Look at the histogram and pick τ by eye. This works surprisingly often (for a single image, anyway). Its weakness is that it assumes the same grey value means the same thing everywhere in the picture, so if one side of the scene is lit more brightly than the other, a single τ will be too low on one side and too high on the other. The lecture points out that MRI scanners have exactly this kind of slowly varying bias across the image.
The percentile method. Suppose we happen to know that the object takes up a fraction p of the picture (maybe it’s a printed character and we know roughly how much ink a character uses). Then we don’t even need the histogram’s shape. If there are n pixels, we declare the m = pn darkest ones to be the object, which is the same thing as setting τ at the p-th quantile of the grey values.

def percentile_threshold(gray, p):
    """The object is assumed dark and to cover a fraction p of the image."""
    return np.quantile(gray, p)

The mode method. Here we take the two-hump picture seriously. We look for two peaks gi and gj in the histogram with a valley gk between them, and we measure how pronounced the valley is with the peakiness
\[
p(i,j,k) = \frac{\min\{H(g_i),\, H(g_j)\}}{H(g_k)} .
\]
Two tall peaks with a deep valley give a large value, so we try every pair of peaks, keep the one with the largest peakiness, and set τ = gk. The method needs the object and background to be fairly uniform and the object to not be too small (otherwise its hump just gets lost in the noise). Real histograms are pretty jagged, so it helps to smooth them a little first, or else every tiny wiggle counts as a peak.

def mode_threshold(hist):
    h = np.convolve(hist, np.ones(5) / 5, mode="same")    # light smoothing
    peaks = [g for g in range(1, 255)
             if h[g] > 0 and h[g] >= h[g - 1] and h[g] >= h[g + 1]]
    best_T, best_p = None, 0.0
    for i in peaks:
        for j in peaks:
            if j <= i:
                continue
            k = i + np.argmin(h[i:j + 1])                  # the valley between them
            p = min(h[i], h[j]) / max(h[k], 1.0)           # avoid dividing by zero
            if p > best_p:
                best_T, best_p = k, p
    return best_T

The iterative method. Start with τ equal to the mean grey value, split the pixels into those below τ and those above, compute the mean of each group, μbelow and μabove, and move τ to the midpoint between them. Then repeat until τ stops moving. This procedure is usually credited to Ridler and Calvard in 1978.

def iterative_threshold(gray, tol=0.5):
    T = gray.mean()
    while True:
        mu_below = gray[gray <= T].mean()
        mu_above = gray[gray > T].mean()
        T_new = 0.5 * (mu_below + mu_above)
        if abs(T_new - T) < tol:
            return T_new
        T = T_new

It’s worth seeing why this is a sensible thing to do, since the slides kind of state it without any motivation. Suppose we want to summarize all the grey values with just two numbers, a dark value μ₁ and a light value μ₂, and assign each pixel to whichever one is closer. The natural measure of how well we’ve done is the total squared error
\[
J = \sum_{g \le \tau} (g - \mu_1)^2 + \sum_{g > \tau} (g - \mu_2)^2 .
\]
If we hold τ fixed and minimize over μ₁, setting the derivative to zero gives μ₁ equal to the mean of the dark group, and similarly for μ₂. If instead we hold μ₁ and μ₂ fixed, each pixel should go to the nearer of the two, and the boundary between “nearer to μ₁” and “nearer to μ₂” is exactly their midpoint. So the iterative method is really just alternating between the two halves of this minimization, and since each step can only lower J, it settles down eventually. (If you’ve seen some machine learning, you’ll probably recognize this as k-means clustering with k = 2, in one dimension.)
To check these against each other we made a test image, a dark ellipse with grey value 60 on a background of 180, plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation 10. The iterative method gave τ ≈ 119 and the mode method gave τ = 102, and both of these sit comfortably in the valley and produce essentially the same binary image.
Adaptive thresholding. When the lighting changes across the image, the honest fix is to let τ change too, which is the idea on the slides of using different thresholds in different regions. A clean way to do this is to compare each pixel with the average of its neighbourhood rather than with one global number, so that if a pixel is clearly darker than its surroundings, it counts as object.

def adaptive_threshold(gray, size=101, C=20):
    """1 where a pixel is darker than (local mean - C)."""
    local_mean = cv2.blur(gray.astype(np.float32), (size, size))
    return (gray < local_mean - C).astype(np.uint8)

OpenCV has the same thing built in as cv2.adaptiveThreshold. On our test image with a brightness ramp of 150 grey levels added from left to right, the single global threshold mislabelled 38% of the pixels, while the adaptive versions mislabelled under 2% (the small differences between our function and OpenCV’s come from how each one treats the borders of the picture). The size of the neighbourhood matters here though. It should be noticeably bigger than the object, otherwise the local mean inside a large dark object is itself dark and the middle of the object just disappears.

Exercise 1.2.1 (Thresholds from the histogram alone) Our iterative_threshold looks at every pixel on every pass, but the two means it needs actually only depend on the histogram, so the whole computation can be done on 256 numbers instead of tens of thousands of pixels. Write iterative_threshold_hist(hist), which does exactly that. The mean grey value of all the pixels with values from g₁ to g₂ is
\[
\bar{g} = \frac{\sum_{g=g_1}^{g_2} g\,H(g)}{\sum_{g=g_1}^{g_2} H(g)} .
\]
The check compares your answer with iterative_threshold(gray) on the test ellipse of this section, so run the cells above first.


def iterative_threshold_hist(hist, tol=0.5):
    """The iterative threshold, computed from a 256-entry histogram only."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    T_pixels = iterative_threshold(gray)
    T_hist = iterative_threshold_hist(np.bincount(gray.ravel(), minlength=256))
    print(f"from the pixels {T_pixels:.3f}, from the histogram {T_hist:.3f}")
    return abs(T_pixels - T_hist) < 0.5

check("Exercise 1.2.1", test)

1.2.2 Projections and a quick bounding box
So now we have a binary image, and the first task in the slides is a very practical one, which is to find a box around the object (Betke, Jan 25 2024, slides 6 to 10). The trick is to count. For each row y we count the object pixels in that row, and for each column x we count the object pixels in that column.
\[
P_1(y) = \sum_x B(x,y), \qquad P_2(x) = \sum_y B(x,y).
\]
These are called projections, because we’ve squashed the two-dimensional picture onto one axis (sort of like the shadow of an object on a wall). The object’s box runs from the first row where P₁ is nonzero to the last one, and likewise for the columns.

P_rows = B.sum(axis=1)     # P1(y): one count per row
P_cols = B.sum(axis=0)     # P2(x): one count per column

min_count = 3              # ignore rows or columns with only a few stray pixels
rows = np.nonzero(P_rows >= min_count)[0]
cols = np.nonzero(P_cols >= min_count)[0]
top, bottom = rows.min(), rows.max()
left, right = cols.min(), cols.max()

cv2.rectangle(img, (left, top), (right, bottom), (0, 255, 0), 2)   # note (x, y) order

The min_count line is there because of a point the slides really stress. The background might contain a few dark pixels of its own, and a single stray pixel near the edge of the picture would otherwise stretch the box all the way out to it, so a threshold on the projections themselves is the cheapest defence.
Projections are more useful than they look. Freeman and colleagues built interactive games that tracked a player’s hand with exactly these sums, and they point out that every moment we compute below can be obtained from projections alone, with single sums instead of double sums (Freeman et al. 1998, Sidebar 2.1). They even used a custom chip that computed the projections in hardware.

Exercise 1.2.2 (More than one box) Projections can find several objects at once, as long as the objects don’t overlap when squashed onto an axis. Write runs(profile, min_count), which returns a list of (start, end) pairs, one for each stretch of consecutive entries of a projection that are at least min_count (both ends count as part of the run). The check builds an image with a disc and a rectangle side by side, finds the runs in its column projection, and then, for each run, uses the row projection of just that vertical strip to finish off the box.


def runs(profile, min_count=1):
    """List of (start, end) index pairs, inclusive, where profile >= min_count."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    pic = np.zeros((160, 300), np.uint8)
    cv2.circle(pic, (70, 80), 40, 1, -1)
    cv2.rectangle(pic, (180, 30), (260, 120), 1, -1)
    col_runs = runs(pic.sum(axis=0), 1)
    print("column runs:", col_runs)
    boxes = []
    for left, right in col_runs:
        strip = pic[:, left:right + 1]
        (top, bottom), = runs(strip.sum(axis=1), 1)
        boxes.append((left, top, right, bottom))
    print("boxes (left, top, right, bottom):", boxes)
    shown = cv2.cvtColor(pic * 255, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2BGR)
    for left, top, right, bottom in boxes:
        cv2.rectangle(shown, (left, top), (right, bottom), (0, 0, 255), 1)
    plt.imshow(shown[:, :, ::-1]); plt.axis("off"); plt.show()
    return col_runs == [(30, 110), (180, 260)] and boxes == [(30, 40, 110, 120), (180, 30, 260, 120)]

check("Exercise 1.2.2", test)

1.2.3 Area and position
Now we start actually measuring the shape, following Horn’s Chapter 3. Think of the object as a flat plate of uniform density cut out of sheet metal, with B as its density, and then the obvious first questions are how much metal there is and where it balances.
The area is the total mass,
\[
A = \sum_x \sum_y B(x,y).
\]
The slides call this the zeroth moment. The general moment of order (p, q) is
\[
M_{pq} = \sum_x \sum_y x^p \, y^q \, B(x,y),
\]
so A = M₀₀. The centroid (or centre of mass) comes from the first moments,
\[
\bar{x} = \frac{M_{10}}{M_{00}} = \frac{1}{A}\sum_x\sum_y x\,B(x,y), \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{M_{01}}{M_{00}} = \frac{1}{A}\sum_x\sum_y y\,B(x,y).
\]
This is just the average x and average y over all the object pixels, and there’s a nice way to see why the average is the right notion of “position”. Ask for the point (x₀, y₀) that’s closest to the object overall, in the sense of minimizing the summed squared distance
\[
S(x_0, y_0) = \sum_x \sum_y \left[ (x - x_0)^2 + (y - y_0)^2 \right] B(x,y).
\]
Setting ∂S/∂x₀ = 0 gives −2 Σ (x − x₀) B = 0, so x₀ Σ B = Σ x B, which is x₀ = x̄, and the same thing holds for y. So the centroid is the unique point that minimizes the spread of the object around it. We’ll see this kind of argument again in a moment, where it ends up doing a lot more work.
In code, the cleanest approach is to ask NumPy for the coordinates of all the object pixels and average them (remember from Section 1.1.3 that np.nonzero gives back rows first).

rows, cols = np.nonzero(B)       # coordinates of every pixel where B == 1
x = cols.astype(float)           # x is the column
y = rows.astype(float)           # y is the row (pointing down!)

A = len(x)
x_bar = x.mean()
y_bar = y.mean()



1.2.4 Orientation
Position and size aren’t enough to tell a pencil lying flat from a pencil standing up, so we want a direction. The natural candidate is the line through the object that it’s “most spread along”, which Horn calls the axis of least second moment (in the mechanical picture, it’s the axis about which the metal plate is easiest to spin).
So we need a way to describe a line and a way to measure how spread out the object is about it. Horn writes a line in the form
\[
x \sin\theta - y \cos\theta + \rho = 0 .
\]
The vector (sin θ, −cos θ) is a unit vector perpendicular to the line, so the line itself points along (cos θ, sin θ) and makes angle θ with the x axis. The nice thing about this form is that if we plug any point (x, y) into the left-hand side, we get its signed perpendicular distance r from the line, and it sidesteps the problem with y = mx + c, whose slope m is infinite for a vertical line. (The class poll on the slides, which asks which of four line equations is wrong, is testing exactly this kind of fluency with the different forms.)
The second moment of the object about the line is the sum of squared distances,
\[
E(\theta, \rho) = \sum_x \sum_y \left( x \sin\theta - y\cos\theta + \rho \right)^2 B(x,y).
\]
We want the line, so both θ and ρ, that makes E as small as possible, and we’ll do it in two steps.
Step one, the offset. Differentiate with respect to ρ and set the result to zero.
\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial \rho} = 2\sum_x\sum_y \left( x\sin\theta - y\cos\theta + \rho\right)B(x,y) = 2A\left(\bar{x}\sin\theta - \bar{y}\cos\theta + \rho\right) = 0 .
\]
The bracket on the right is the line equation evaluated at the centroid, so whatever the angle is, the best line passes through the centroid. That settles ρ, and it also tells us that the axis of most second moment (the one we’d get by maximizing over θ instead) goes through the centroid too.
Step two, the angle. Since the line goes through (x̄, ȳ), it’s convenient to measure everything from there, so define the centred coordinates x′ = x − x̄ and y′ = y − ȳ. In these coordinates ρ = 0 and the distance is just r = x′ sin θ − y′ cos θ. Expanding the square,
\[
E(\theta) = \sin^2\theta \sum x'^2 B \; - \; 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \sum x'y' B \; + \; \cos^2\theta \sum y'^2 B .
\]
The three sums only depend on the shape (not on θ), so we give them names. Following Horn,
\[
a = \sum_x\sum_y x'^2\, B(x,y), \qquad b = 2\sum_x\sum_y x'y'\, B(x,y), \qquad c = \sum_x\sum_y y'^2\, B(x,y).
\]
These are the second central moments, and the factor of 2 in b is just a convention that tidies up the formulas below. Now
\[
E(\theta) = a\sin^2\theta - b\sin\theta\cos\theta + c\cos^2\theta .
\]
The double angle identities sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2, cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2 and sin θ cos θ = (sin 2θ)/2 turn this into
\[
E(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{2}(a+c) \; - \; \tfrac{1}{2}(a-c)\cos 2\theta \; - \; \tfrac{1}{2}\, b \sin 2\theta .
\]
The slides write this without the factors of one half, which is just twice the same function and so has the same minimum (Betke, Jan 25 2024, slide 4). Setting dE/dθ = 0 gives (a − c) sin 2θ = b cos 2θ, in other words
\[
\tan 2\theta = \frac{b}{a-c}.
\]
This has two solutions between 0 and π, a right angle apart, one of which is the minimum and the other the maximum, and the equation alone doesn’t tell us which is which. To find out we use a trick that’s worth remembering, which is that any combination of cos 2θ and sin 2θ can be written as a single shifted cosine. Define
\[
R = \sqrt{b^2 + (a-c)^2}, \qquad \cos\varphi = \frac{a-c}{R}, \qquad \sin\varphi = \frac{b}{R}.
\]
Then (a − c) cos 2θ + b sin 2θ = R cos(2θ − φ), and
\[
E(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{2}(a+c) - \tfrac{1}{2}R\cos(2\theta - \varphi).
\]
Now everything is visible at a glance. E is smallest when the cosine equals +1, at 2θ = φ, and largest when it equals −1, a quarter turn later, so the minimizing angle is θ = φ/2, where φ is the angle whose cosine and sine are proportional to a − c and b. And that’s precisely what the two-argument arctangent computes.

xp = x - x_bar                 # centred coordinates
yp = y - y_bar
a = np.sum(xp * xp)
b = 2 * np.sum(xp * yp)
c = np.sum(yp * yp)

theta = 0.5 * np.arctan2(b, a - c)      # angle of the axis of least second moment

Here’s a pitfall that has nothing to do with images and everything to do with trigonometry. If you write np.arctan(b / (a - c)) instead, you only get the right answer when a > c. When a < c the one-argument arctangent lands in the wrong quadrant and you get the axis of most second moment, perpendicular to the true one (and when a = c it divides by zero). The two-argument arctan2 keeps track of the signs separately and always picks the minimum. Freeman and colleagues use exactly this formula, θ = ½ arctan(b, a − c), to read off the orientation of a hand (Freeman et al. 1998, Sidebar 2.1).
The second pitfall is the one we promised back in Section 1.1.3. Our y is the row index, which points down. The formula doesn’t care, it just gives the angle from the x axis toward the y axis, but on the screen that’s a clockwise angle, so an object that looks tilted 30° counter-clockwise will report θ = −30°. If you only use θ to draw the axis back onto the same image, everything is consistent and you don’t need to do anything, but if you report the angle to a human, flip its sign.

# Draw the axis through the centroid, 100 pixels each way.
dx, dy = 100 * np.cos(theta), 100 * np.sin(theta)
p1 = (int(x_bar - dx), int(y_bar - dy))
p2 = (int(x_bar + dx), int(y_bar + dy))
cv2.line(img, p1, p2, (0, 0, 255), 2)

print("angle as a human would see it:", -np.degrees(theta), "degrees")

angle as a human would see it: -29.975183217375708 degrees


As a check, OpenCV computes the same central moments for us. In its naming, mu20 is our a, mu02 is our c, and mu11 is half of our b.

m = cv2.moments(B, binaryImage=True)
x_bar, y_bar = m["m10"] / m["m00"], m["m01"] / m["m00"]
a, b, c = m["mu20"], 2 * m["mu11"], m["mu02"]

We drew a filled ellipse with OpenCV at an angle of 30° and ran both versions on it, and they agreed to every printed digit, giving θ = 29.98°.


1.2.5 Round or elongated?
The angle tells us which way the object points, but not how strongly it points. A disc technically has an orientation too, but it doesn’t mean anything, since every axis through the centre gives the same E. This suggests comparing the smallest and largest values of E, which we can read off directly from the shifted-cosine form,
\[
E_{\min} = \tfrac{1}{2}(a+c) - \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{b^2 + (a-c)^2}, \qquad E_{\max} = \tfrac{1}{2}(a+c) + \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{b^2 + (a-c)^2}.
\]
The ratio
\[
\text{roundness} = \frac{E_{\min}}{E_{\max}}
\]
lies between 0 and 1. It’s 1 for anything as symmetric as a disc or a square, where a = c and b = 0, and it goes to 0 for a long thin line. The slides call it the circularity measure, and use it to tell the American Sign Language letters A and B apart, since a fist is compact and an open flat hand is elongated (Betke, Jan 25 2024, slides 4 and 5). The same idea separates round red blood cells from elongated sickle cells under a microscope.
It isn’t obvious from the formula that Emin can never be negative (though of course it can’t, since it’s a sum of squares), and it’s a nice exercise to see this directly. Multiply out
\[
(a+c)^2 - \left[b^2 + (a-c)^2\right] = 4ac - b^2 = 4\left[ \left(\sum x'^2 B\right)\left(\sum y'^2 B\right) - \left(\sum x'y' B\right)^2 \right] .
\]
The bracket is non-negative by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, so a + c is at least as big as the square root and Emin ≥ 0. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz needs y′ to be proportional to x′ for every object pixel, which means every pixel lies on a single straight line through the centroid, so only an infinitely thin line has roundness zero.
There’s a deeper way to look at all of this, and it connects these formulas to basically the rest of applied mathematics. Collect the second moments into a symmetric matrix and write the line’s unit normal as n,
\[
C = \begin{pmatrix} a & b/2 \\ b/2 & c \end{pmatrix}, \qquad n = \begin{pmatrix} \sin\theta \\ -\cos\theta \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Multiplying out shows that E(θ) = nᵀ C n. Minimizing nᵀ C n over unit vectors is the textbook eigenvalue problem, so Emin and Emax are just the two eigenvalues of C (and indeed the standard formula for the eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 symmetric matrix is ½(a + c) ± ½√((a − c)² + b²), which is exactly what we found). The axis of least second moment is perpendicular to the eigenvector for Emin, so it points along the eigenvector for Emax. Up to a factor of the area, C is the covariance matrix of the pixel coordinates, so finding the main axis of an object is really just principal component analysis applied to its pixels. The Wikipedia article on image moments states the same connection in its second set of examples.
The eigenvalues also tell us how big the object is along each axis. For a uniformly filled ellipse with semi-axes α and β, a short calculation gives second moments (π/4)αβ³ and (π/4)α³β about its two axes, and area παβ. Dividing,
\[
\frac{E_{\min}}{A} = \frac{\beta^2}{4}, \qquad \frac{E_{\max}}{A} = \frac{\alpha^2}{4},
\]
so the semi-axes of the equivalent ellipse (the ellipse with the same zeroth, first and second moments as our object) are 2√(Emin/A) and 2√(Emax/A), and the roundness of an ellipse is therefore (β/α)².

R = np.sqrt(b**2 + (a - c)**2)
E_min = 0.5 * (a + c) - 0.5 * R
E_max = 0.5 * (a + c) + 0.5 * R

roundness = E_min / E_max
semi_major = 2 * np.sqrt(E_max / A)
semi_minor = 2 * np.sqrt(E_min / A)

Our test ellipse had semi-axes 80 and 25 pixels, and the code recovered 80.5 and 25.4, with a roundness of 0.0998 against the exact (25/80)² = 0.0977. The small excess comes from the noise and from the jagged staircase edge of a digital ellipse, which adds a little bit of width.
It’s worth stepping back for a second to notice what we’ve done. With six sums over the pixels we can say how big an object is, where it is, which way it points and how elongated it is, and that’s enough to steer a game character with your hand, which is exactly what Freeman’s group did in the late 1990s on hardware far slower than a modern phone. But it only works when there’s one object in the picture, since with several of them the sums just mix them all together. We’ll need a way to pull separate blobs apart, and that problem comes back in Section 1.4, when several children move around the KidsRoom at once.

Exercise 1.2.3 (A shape summary) Let’s gather Section 1.2 into one function. Write shape_stats(B), which takes a binary image and returns a dictionary with four entries. "area" is A, "centroid" is the pair (x̄, ȳ), "angle" is the orientation in degrees as a human would read it, counter-clockwise from the x axis (so remember the sign flip of Section 1.2.4), and "roundness" is Emin/Emax. The check draws ellipses at known angles with OpenCV, whose own angle argument turns clockwise on the screen, and a disc.


def shape_stats(B):
    """Area, centroid, orientation (degrees, counter-clockwise) and roundness of a binary image."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    ok = True
    for cv_angle in [0, 30, 75, 120]:
        pic = np.zeros((240, 240), np.uint8)
        cv2.ellipse(pic, (120, 110), (80, 25), cv_angle, 0, 360, 1, -1)
        s = shape_stats(pic)
        expected = -cv_angle
        off = (s["angle"] - expected + 90) % 180 - 90          # angles of an axis repeat every 180 degrees
        print(f"OpenCV angle {cv_angle:3d}:  your angle {s['angle']:7.2f}   roundness {s['roundness']:.4f}   centroid ({s['centroid'][0]:.1f}, {s['centroid'][1]:.1f})")
        ok = ok and abs(off) < 0.5 and abs(s["roundness"] - (25 / 80) ** 2) < 0.01
        ok = ok and abs(s["centroid"][0] - 120) < 0.5 and abs(s["centroid"][1] - 110) < 0.5
    disc = np.zeros((101, 101), np.uint8)
    cv2.circle(disc, (50, 50), 40, 1, -1)
    d = shape_stats(disc)
    print(f"disc: area {d['area']}, roundness {d['roundness']:.4f}")
    return ok and d["area"] == int(disc.sum()) and d["roundness"] > 0.99

Exercise 1.2.4 (Moments from projections) Freeman and colleagues computed every moment up to second order from projections, which their retina chip could produce in hardware. First convince yourself that A, M₁₀ and M₂₀ are all sums over the column projection alone (for instance M₂₀ = Σ x² P₂(x)), and that the row projection gives M₀₁ and M₀₂ in the same way. The cross moment M₁₁ is harder, because it mixes x and y, and the trick is a third projection, along diagonals. Let D(d) be the number of object pixels with x + y = d, and show that
\[
\sum_d d^2 D(d) = M_{20} + 2M_{11} + M_{02},
\]
so that M₁₁ follows from the three projections. You’ll also need to show that the central moments follow from the raw ones, for instance a = M₂₀ − A x̄². Then write moments_from_projections(B), which returns (A, x̄, ȳ, a, b, c) using only P₁, P₂ and D. A hint for D is that np.bincount(rows + cols) counts how many object pixels lie on each diagonal. The check compares your numbers with OpenCV’s moments of the test ellipse.

def test():

    m = cv2.moments(B, binaryImage=True)
    theirs = (m["m00"], m["m10"] / m["m00"], m["m01"] / m["m00"], m["mu20"], 2 * m["mu11"], m["mu02"])
    for name, mine, ref in zip(["A", "x_bar", "y_bar", "a", "b", "c"], (A, x_bar, y_bar, a, b, c), theirs):

1.3 Finding a Face
Lecture notes 2 sets itself a concrete goal, which is to take a frame from a webcam, find the face in it and say how big it is (Lecture notes 2). This is the problem behind the Camera Mouse, the system from Betke’s group that lets people with severe motor disabilities steer a cursor with their head, and it’s a good problem to learn on because it’s hard in instructive ways (faces come in lots of sizes and turn up in front of cluttered backgrounds, as slide 17 shows). The lecture attacks it with two complementary ideas. The first one uses colour, which is cheap and rough, and the second compares the picture against a template, which is expensive and precise, and at the end the two get combined.

1.3.1 Skin colour
The simplest idea is right there in the title of slide 3, which is to find every pixel whose colour looks like skin and hope that the largest skin-coloured blob is the face. Once we have a binary skin mask, everything from Section 1.2 applies, so we can find the box with projections, exactly as for the bat (which is how the January 25 lecture presents it, Betke, Jan 25 2024, slides 14 and 15), or we can keep only the largest connected blob.
The question is what “looks like skin” should even mean. Raw RGB values are a poor choice, because the same cheek gives very different numbers in shadow and in sunlight. Slide 16 of the January 25 deck shows the standard fix, a plot of normalized red against normalized green, taken from Shapiro and Stockman’s Computer Vision. These are
\[
r = \frac{R}{R+G+B}, \qquad g = \frac{G}{R+G+B}.
\]
(There’s no need for a normalized blue, since r + g + b = 1 and the third number doesn’t carry any new information.) The point of dividing by R + G + B is easy to see. If the light falling on a patch of skin gets brighter or dimmer by some factor k, all three channels get multiplied by k, and k cancels from top and bottom, so r and g describe the hue of a pixel and ignore its brightness. Our test patch with (R, G, B) = (200, 150, 120) and the same patch at half brightness both gave r = 0.426 and g = 0.319. A well-known empirical observation is that skin of very different tones clusters tightly in the (r, g) plane, because a lot of the difference between skin tones is a difference in overall brightness, which the normalization removes. On the slide, the face, the shadowed parts of the face and the beard each form their own small cluster.
Rather than memorizing the boundaries of the skin cluster from a book, it’s often more robust to learn them from the person in front of the camera. We cut out a small patch of their cheek, compute the mean and spread of r and g there, and call a pixel skin if it’s within a few standard deviations of that mean.

def chromaticity(img):
    """Normalized red and green for every pixel of a BGR image."""
    img = img.astype(float)                 # avoid uint8 overflow in the sum!
    total = img.sum(axis=2) + 1e-6          # tiny number avoids dividing by zero on black pixels
    r = img[:, :, 2] / total
    g = img[:, :, 1] / total
    return r, g

def skin_model(patch):
    r, g = chromaticity(patch)
    return r.mean(), r.std(), g.mean(), g.std()

def skin_mask(img, model, k=2.5):
    r_mean, r_std, g_mean, g_std = model
    r, g = chromaticity(img)
    close_in_r = np.abs(r - r_mean) < k * r_std
    close_in_g = np.abs(g - g_mean) < k * g_std
    return (close_in_r & close_in_g).astype(np.uint8)

Notice the astype(float) at the top of chromaticity. Adding three uint8 channels together is exactly the overflow trap of Section 1.1.5, since 200 + 150 + 120 is already past 255. With the mask in hand we keep the biggest blob, and OpenCV will label the blobs and measure them for us in one call (we’ll see how that kind of labelling actually works in Section 1.4.3).


Setup: load the test scene
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. Load the synthetic scene made at the top of this chapter.
frame = cv2.imread("face.jpg")



model = skin_model(frame[110:130, 190:210])     # a patch we know is cheek
M = skin_mask(frame, model)

n, labels, stats, centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(M, connectivity=8)
areas = stats[1:, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA]           # row 0 is the background, so skip it
face = 1 + np.argmax(areas)                     # label of the largest blob
x, y, w, h = stats[face, :4]                    # its bounding box
cv2.rectangle(frame, (x, y), (x + w, y + h), (0, 255, 0), 2)

On a synthetic test scene with an unevenly lit skin-coloured ellipse, this found 5,280 of the ellipse’s 5,403 pixels and put the box in the right place.
Colour is fast, and it doesn’t care about the size or pose of the face, but its weaknesses are just as clear. Anything skin-coloured counts (wooden doors are notorious offenders), and hands and arms are skin too, so the largest blob might not be the face at all. The colour of the light also matters, since warm indoor bulbs shift every pixel toward red. So colour is best used to tell us where to look, and then we leave the final verdict to something more careful.

Exercise 1.3.1 (When the light changes colour) Our skin model was learned under one light. Normalizing by R + G + B protected us from the light getting brighter or dimmer, but what if it changes colour? Warm indoor bulbs give out relatively more red and less blue, and the starter cell simulates one by multiplying the red channel of face.jpg by 1.3 and the blue channel by 0.8, clipping at 255. Write face_pixels_found(scene, model), which returns how many pixels inside the true face ellipse, true_face, the skin mask finds. The check compares three cases, the original model on the original scene, the original model under the warm light, and a model re-learned from the same cheek patch under the warm light. Before running it, try to predict which case fails, and why the normalization doesn’t help there.


# [Exercise setup] The warm-light scene and the true face region (no need to change these lines).
original = cv2.imread("face.jpg")
warm = original.astype(float)
warm[:, :, 2] *= 1.3                      # more red
warm[:, :, 0] *= 0.8                      # less blue
warm = np.clip(warm, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
true_face = np.zeros(original.shape[:2], np.uint8)
cv2.ellipse(true_face, (200, 120), (35, 48), 0, 0, 360, 1, -1)

def face_pixels_found(scene, model):
    """Number of pixels inside true_face that skin_mask(scene, model) marks as skin."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    patch = (slice(110, 130), slice(190, 210))
    old_model, new_model = skin_model(original[patch]), skin_model(warm[patch])
    total = int(true_face.sum())
    cases = {"original model, original light": face_pixels_found(original, old_model),
             "original model, warm light": face_pixels_found(warm, old_model),
             "re-learned model, warm light": face_pixels_found(warm, new_model)}
    for name, found in cases.items():
        print(f"{name:32s} found {found:5d} of {total} face pixels")
    reference = int(skin_mask(warm, old_model)[true_face == 1].sum())
    found = list(cases.values())
    return found[1] == reference and found[0] > 0.75 * total and found[2] > 0.75 * total and found[1] < 0.25 * total

1.3.2 Template matching with the sum of squared differences
The second idea is more literal. We take a small picture of a face, the template, slide it over every position in the scene, and at each position measure how different the scene looks from the template, and then the position where they differ the least is our answer.
Slide 8 makes this precise. Let the template m and the piece of scene underneath it, s, both have n pixels, and write their i-th pixels as mi and si. The sum of squared differences is
\[
\text{SSD} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (s_i - m_i)^2 .
\]
It’s zero for a perfect match and grows as the two differ, so template matching is really just an exhaustive search for the position with the smallest SSD. Written out as plainly as possible, it’s two loops over positions with a sum inside.


Setup: a textured test image and a template
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. A textured grey test image, and a template cut out of it.
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
gray = cv2.GaussianBlur(rng.uniform(0, 255, (120, 160)), (0, 0), 2)
gray = cv2.normalize(gray, None, 0, 255, cv2.NORM_MINMAX).astype(np.uint8)
template = gray[40:60, 70:95].copy()



def ssd_map(image, template):
    """SSD between the template and every window of a grey image."""
    image = image.astype(float)
    template = template.astype(float)
    H, W = image.shape
    h, w = template.shape
    out = np.zeros((H - h + 1, W - w + 1))
    for y in range(H - h + 1):
        for x in range(W - w + 1):
            window = image[y:y + h, x:x + w]
            out[y, x] = np.sum((window - template) ** 2)
    return out

scores = ssd_map(gray, template)
y, x = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(scores), scores.shape)   # best position (row, col)

The result is itself an image, a match map, whose value at (x, y) says how well the template fits with its top-left corner there. Slides 6, 7 and 9 show maps like this, with the best match as a single marked pixel. The map is smaller than the scene by the template size minus one, because the template has to fit inside.
This loop is honest but slow. For a 640 × 480 frame and a 50 × 50 template there are about 270,000 positions with 2,500 pixels each, so roughly 7 × 10⁸ subtractions per frame, and even with NumPy doing each inner sum, our loop took about 1.7 seconds on a 640 × 480 test frame (which is pretty hopeless for video arriving 30 times a second). OpenCV’s cv2.matchTemplate does the same computation in optimized code. With the method cv2.TM_SQDIFF it returns exactly our SSD map, and on our tests the two agreed to about six significant figures, and on the same 640 × 480 frame OpenCV ran the normalized search of the next subsection in about 7 milliseconds.

scores = cv2.matchTemplate(gray.astype(np.float32), template.astype(np.float32), cv2.TM_SQDIFF)

SSD has a serious weakness though, and it shows up when we expand the square,
\[
\text{SSD} = \sum_i s_i^2 \; - \; 2\sum_i s_i m_i \; + \; \sum_i m_i^2 .
\]
The last term is the same everywhere. The middle term, the cross-correlation, is the part that measures whether bright pixels in the template line up with bright pixels in the scene, which is what we actually care about. But the first term only depends on how bright the scene is under the template, so brightness alone moves the score around. Suppose the face in the scene is identical to the template except that the room light is dimmer, so that si = mi − c for every pixel. Then SSD = nc², which can be enormous even though the pattern is a perfect match. In our test we cut a template from an image and then darkened that spot of the image (as a shadow would), halving its contrast and shifting its brightness, and SSD then picked a completely different location. So what we need is a score that ignores brightness and contrast.

Exercise 1.3.2 (SSD without the loops) NumPy can actually hand us every window of an image at once. The function np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(image, template.shape) returns an array of shape (H − h + 1, W − w + 1, h, w) whose entry [y, x] is the window with top-left corner (x, y), without copying a single pixel. Use it to write ssd_map_fast(image, template) with no Python loops at all. The check compares it with ssd_map on the textured test image and times both.


def ssd_map_fast(image, template):
    """The same match map as ssd_map, computed without Python loops."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


import time

def test():
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); slow = ssd_map(gray, template); t1 = time.perf_counter()
    fast = ssd_map_fast(gray, template); t2 = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"loops {t1 - t0:.3f} s, sliding windows {t2 - t1:.3f} s")
    return fast.shape == slow.shape and np.allclose(fast, slow)

1.3.3 The normalized correlation coefficient
Slides 10 and 11 give the answer. Let s̄ and σs be the mean and standard deviation of the scene window, and m̄ and σm those of the template. The normalized correlation coefficient is
\[
r = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(s_i - \bar{s})\,(m_i - \bar{m})}{\sigma_s\,\sigma_m}.
\]
If you’ve done some statistics you’ll recognize this as the ordinary correlation coefficient between the two lists of pixel values. The slides make a point of not naming it after Karl Pearson, observing that he didn’t invent it and that he’s remembered for his role in eugenics, and we’ll follow the slides on that.
The formula looks busy, but there’s a pretty simple idea hiding in it. Define the standardized pixel values
\[
\hat{s}_i = \frac{s_i - \bar{s}}{\sigma_s}, \qquad \hat{m}_i = \frac{m_i - \bar{m}}{\sigma_m}.
\]
Each list now has mean zero and standard deviation one, and the coefficient is just their average product, r = (1/n) Σ ŝi m̂i. Standardizing is where all the work happens. Suppose the lighting changes so that every scene pixel becomes asi + b, with a > 0 changing the contrast and b the brightness. The mean becomes a s̄ + b and the standard deviation becomes a σs, and so
\[
\frac{(a s_i + b) - (a\bar{s} + b)}{a\,\sigma_s} = \frac{s_i - \bar{s}}{\sigma_s} = \hat{s}_i .
\]
Both a and b have vanished, so the normalized correlation is completely blind to brightness and contrast changes, which is exactly the property SSD was missing. In our shadow test it found the right location with r = 1.000.
Two more facts make r pleasant to work with. First, it always lies between −1 and 1, since Σ ŝi² = n and Σ m̂i² = n, so the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives |Σ ŝi m̂i| ≤ n, which is |r| ≤ 1. It reaches 1 only when the standardized patches are identical, and −1 for a photographic negative. So unlike SSD, whose size depends on the template, r comes with a built-in scale, and a value of 0.9 means a good match in any picture, which means we can set a threshold below which we say there’s no face at all.
Second, r is secretly an SSD after all. Expand the squared difference of the standardized patches,
\[
\sum_i (\hat{s}_i - \hat{m}_i)^2 = \sum_i \hat{s}_i^2 + \sum_i \hat{m}_i^2 - 2\sum_i \hat{s}_i\hat{m}_i = n + n - 2nr = 2n(1 - r).
\]
So maximizing r is the same as minimizing the SSD between standardized patches. We haven’t thrown anything away, we’ve just decided to compare patterns after removing brightness and contrast (which is what we wanted all along).
In code, the only change from the SSD loop is the standardization, plus a guard for perfectly flat windows, whose standard deviation is zero.

def ncc_map(image, template):
    image = image.astype(float)
    template = template.astype(float)
    H, W = image.shape
    h, w = template.shape
    t = (template - template.mean()) / template.std()      # standardize once
    out = np.zeros((H - h + 1, W - w + 1))
    for y in range(H - h + 1):
        for x in range(W - w + 1):
            window = image[y:y + h, x:x + w]
            sd = window.std()
            if sd == 0:              # a flat patch matches nothing
                continue
            s = (window - window.mean()) / sd
            out[y, x] = np.mean(s * t)
    return out

OpenCV’s version is the method cv2.TM_CCOEFF_NORMED. It computes the same quantity, and on our test the maps agreed to six decimal places. Note that here the best match is the maximum, not the minimum.

R = cv2.matchTemplate(gray.astype(np.float32), template.astype(np.float32), cv2.TM_CCOEFF_NORMED)
min_val, max_val, min_loc, max_loc = cv2.minMaxLoc(R)
x, y = max_loc                  # minMaxLoc returns (x, y), not (row, col)!
if max_val < 0.6:
    print("no convincing match")

That last comment is Section 1.1.3 striking again, since np.argmax with np.unravel_index gives (row, column), while cv2.minMaxLoc gives (x, y).
So which face should the template be? Slide 7 uses the face of one particular student, which works well for that student and less well for everyone else. Slides 9 and 12 use an average face, made by lining up lots of photographs of faces and averaging them pixel by pixel. The average blurs away individual features and keeps what all faces share (dark eye sockets above bright cheeks, for example), and it makes a much better generic template. Freeman and colleagues used normalized correlation for the same reason in their small-object tracker (Freeman et al. 1998, Sidebar 5.1).

Exercise 1.3.3 (What normalized correlation forgives) Write ssd(s, m) and ncc(s, m) for two patches of the same shape, following the formulas of Sections 1.3.2 and 1.3.3. Use the population standard deviation, which is what np.std gives by default, since it matches the 1/n in the formula. The check takes a patch m and makes altered copies a·m + b for several contrasts a and brightness shifts b, including a = −1, and prints both scores, and then it tests the identity Σ(ŝᵢ − m̂ᵢ)² = 2n(1 − r) on a random pair of patches. Take a good look at the printed table. Which changes does r ignore completely, and what happens to SSD?


def ssd(s, m):
    """Sum of squared differences between two patches of the same shape."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError

def ncc(s, m):
    """Normalized correlation coefficient between two patches of the same shape."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
    m = rng.uniform(0, 255, (20, 25))
    ok = True
    print("    a      b          SSD       r")
    for a, b in [(1, 0), (1, 40), (0.5, 0), (0.5, 60), (2, -30), (-1, 255)]:
        s = a * m + b
        r = ncc(s, m)
        print(f"{a:5.1f} {b:6.0f} {ssd(s, m):12.0f} {r:7.3f}")
        ok = ok and abs(r - np.sign(a)) < 1e-9
    s, t = rng.normal(size=(10, 10)), rng.normal(size=(10, 10))
    r = ncc(s, t)
    s_hat = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
    t_hat = (t - t.mean()) / t.std()
    lhs, rhs = np.sum((s_hat - t_hat) ** 2), 2 * s.size * (1 - r)
    print(f"identity: left side {lhs:.6f}, right side {rhs:.6f}")
    return ok and abs(lhs - rhs) < 1e-9 and abs(r - np.corrcoef(s.ravel(), t.ravel())[0, 1]) < 1e-9 and ssd(m, m) == 0
