title: 3  Tracking, Edges and Optical Flow
text:
3.5 Optical Flow

3.5.1 Brightness constancy
Frame differencing in Section 1.4.2 told us where things changed between two frames, and optical flow asks for more, which is how each pixel moved, as a vector (u, v) per pixel. The two classic methods, both from 1981, are the ones the schedule lists for this lecture, Horn and Schunck’s and Lucas and Kanade’s.
Both start from the same assumption, brightness constancy, which says that a point keeps its brightness as it moves. If the point at (x, y) at time t moves to (x + u δt, y + v δt) at time t + δt, then
\[
I(x + u\,\delta t,\; y + v\,\delta t,\; t + \delta t) = I(x, y, t).
\]
Expand the left side to first order in δt, cancel I(x, y, t), and divide by δt,
\[
I_x\,u + I_y\,v + I_t = 0 ,
\]
where Ix, Iy and It are the partial derivatives of the brightness. This is the optical flow constraint equation, and it’s the starting point for both methods. In practice Ix and Iy come from masks like the ones in Section 3.3.1 and It from the difference between the two frames.


3.5.2 The aperture problem
There’s a catch, which is that the constraint is one equation in two unknowns. Geometrically, it says (u, v) lies on a line in the (u, v) plane, perpendicular to the gradient (Ix, Iy), so it fixes the component of the motion along the gradient,
\[
\text{normal flow} = -\frac{I_t}{\sqrt{I_x^2 + I_y^2}},
\]
and leaves the component along the edge completely undetermined. That’s the aperture problem, and you’ve probably seen it in the barber pole illusion, where stripes on a rotating pole seem to move up even though the surface moves sideways, since looking at a straight edge through a small window, you can only see it move perpendicular to itself. So to get the full flow we need to bring in more information, and the two methods do it in different ways. Horn and Schunck assume the flow is smooth across the whole image, and Lucas and Kanade assume it’s constant in a small window.


3.5.3 Horn and Schunck
Horn and Schunck look for the flow field that satisfies the constraint as well as possible while varying smoothly, by minimizing
\[
E(u, v) = \iint \Big[(I_x u + I_y v + I_t)^2 + \lambda\big(\|\nabla u\|^2 + \|\nabla v\|^2\big)\Big]\,dx\,dy ,
\]
where λ sets how much we care about smoothness. The Euler-Lagrange equations of this functional are
\[
I_x(I_x u + I_y v + I_t) = \lambda\nabla^2 u, \qquad I_y(I_x u + I_y v + I_t) = \lambda\nabla^2 v .
\]
On the grid, the Laplacian is approximated as ∇²u ≈ κ(ū − u), where ū is a local average of u over the neighbours (with κ a constant that depends on the averaging mask, which we fold into λ). Substituting and solving the two linear equations for u and v at each pixel gives the famous update
\[
u \leftarrow \bar{u} - I_x\,\frac{I_x\bar{u} + I_y\bar{v} + I_t}{\lambda + I_x^2 + I_y^2}, \qquad v \leftarrow \bar{v} - I_y\,\frac{I_x\bar{u} + I_y\bar{v} + I_t}{\lambda + I_x^2 + I_y^2},
\]
which we iterate, recomputing the averages each time. There’s a nice reading of it. Each pixel starts from the average of its neighbours and then moves along the gradient direction just enough to (nearly) satisfy its own constraint, so in places with strong gradients the data decides, and in flat regions, where Ix and Iy are small, the flow is just filled in from the surroundings. That filling in is what solves the aperture problem, but it’s also the method’s weakness, since the smoothness term blurs the flow across the boundaries of moving objects.

The check moves a smooth random texture by a known sub-pixel amount and compares the median flow with the true motion.

# [Setup] Two frames of a smooth random texture; the second is the first shifted by (0.6, -0.4) pixels.
def shifted_pair(du, dv, seed=0, size=(96, 128), blur=4):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    base = cv2.GaussianBlur(rng.uniform(0, 255, size), (0, 0), blur)

    return base, moved
F1, F2 = shifted_pair(0.6, -0.4)

    inner = (slice(15, -15), slice(15, -15))
    mu, mv = np.median(u[inner]), np.median(v[inner])
    print(f"median flow ({mu:.3f}, {mv:.3f}), true (0.6, -0.4)")
    return abs(mu - 0.6) < 0.08 and abs(mv + 0.4) < 0.08

3.5.4 Lucas and Kanade
Lucas and Kanade take the local route. Assume the flow is the same, (u, v), for every pixel in a small window around the point we care about. Each pixel in the window gives one constraint equation, so a 5 × 5 window gives 25 equations in 2 unknowns, and we solve them by least squares. Stacking the gradients into a matrix A with rows (Ix, Iy) and the time derivatives into a vector b with entries −It, we want A(u, v)⊤ ≈ b, and the normal equations are
\[
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \sum I_x^2 & \sum I_x I_y \\ \sum I_x I_y & \sum I_y^2 \end{pmatrix}}_{A^\top A} \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v\end{pmatrix} = -\begin{pmatrix} \sum I_x I_t \\ \sum I_y I_t\end{pmatrix},
\]
with the sums over the window. The 2 × 2 matrix A⊤A, sometimes called the structure tensor, tells us whether the problem can be solved at all. If the window contains gradients in only one direction (a straight edge), A⊤A has one eigenvalue near zero and can’t be inverted, which is just the aperture problem again, and if the window is flat both eigenvalues are tiny. Only when both eigenvalues are reasonably large, at corners and in textured patches, is the flow well determined. That’s exactly the criterion the Harris and Shi-Tomasi corner detectors use to pick “good features to track”, which is not a coincidence, since Shi and Tomasi derived it from this tracking problem.
The constraint equation came from a first-order Taylor expansion, so it only works for small motions, a pixel or so. For larger motions there are two standard fixes, and the usual implementation uses both. One is to iterate, warping the second image by the current flow estimate and solving again for the small leftover motion. The other is the coarse-to-fine idea from Section 1.3.4, solving for the flow on a small pyramid level where the motion is small in pixels, then doubling it and refining on the next level. OpenCV’s cv2.calcOpticalFlowPyrLK is exactly this pyramidal, iterative Lucas-Kanade tracker, and it’s still one of the most used pieces of code in computer vision.

    print(f"texture: flow ({u:.3f}, {v:.3f}), smaller eigenvalue {lam_min:.1f};  edge: smaller eigenvalue {lam_edge:.2e}")

The two methods have stayed popular for different reasons. Lucas-Kanade is fast and local, so it’s what you use to track a few hundred good corners through a video, and Horn-Schunck gives a dense field everywhere, which is what you want for things like segmenting moving objects or estimating motion in medical images. Modern methods replace both with neural networks trained on synthetic videos with known flow, but most of them still use a coarse-to-fine pyramid and some form of the brightness constancy idea inside, so these two papers are still really worth reading.

4.1 Learning From Images
After the midterm the course changes gears. The lectures from March 5 to March 28 bring in deep learning, spend two lectures on faces (recognition, pose, aging, facial expressions and biometrics more generally) and then go back to geometry with binocular and multiview stereo, epipolar geometry, structured light and structure from motion, finishing with deep networks for segmentation (CS 585 schedule). That’s two quite different kinds of computer vision sitting side by side, one that learns everything from data and one that’s built on exact geometry, and the interesting thing about the field right now is how much the two have been mixing. We’ll go through them in the order of the lectures.
A practical note before we start. Deep learning is normally done with PyTorch, which can’t run inside a browser, so the runnable cells in this chapter do everything with NumPy, on problems small enough to train in a few seconds. That’s actually a good way to learn it, since nothing is hidden, and wherever it helps I show the PyTorch version as plain code that you can run on your own computer with start_kernel.py.

title: 4  Deep Learning, Faces and Multiple Views
text:
4.1.1 From hand-made features to learned ones
Everything in the first three chapters was designed by hand. Somebody decided that normalized red and green are good for skin, that the second moments describe a blob’s shape, that the Sobel mask is a good derivative, and each of those choices took real insight. The trouble is that for most recognition problems nobody knows what the right features are. What makes a picture a picture of a dog, as opposed to a cat or a wolf, isn’t something you can write down as a formula, and decades of carefully engineered features only got so far.
The turning point was data. In 2009 Fei-Fei Li’s group released ImageNet, which grew to more than 14 million images labelled with thousands of categories, and from 2010 on it ran a yearly challenge on a 1000-class subset. In 2012 Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton entered a convolutional neural network, now called AlexNet, trained on two gaming GPUs, and got a top-5 error of about 15%, against about 26% for the next best entry, which used hand-designed features. Within a couple of years basically every entry was a neural network, and by 2015 ResNet (He and colleagues) had pushed the error below the rough estimate of human performance on that benchmark. The lesson people took from it is that given enough labelled data and enough computing, it’s better to learn the features than to design them, and that’s what the rest of this section is about.


4.1.2 Convolution layers
A convolutional network is built mostly from one operation that we already know well, which is sliding a small mask over an image and computing a weighted sum at every position. That’s template matching from Section 1.3.2, or the Sobel filter from Section 3.3.1, with one big difference, which is that the weights in the mask aren’t chosen by us, they’re learned. A convolution layer takes an input with Cin channels (3 for a colour image, or many more deeper in the network) and produces Cout output channels, each one the sum over input channels of a filtered version of that channel plus a bias,
\[
y_o(i, j) = b_o + \sum_{c=1}^{C_{\text{in}}} \sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\sum_{n=0}^{k-1} w_{o,c}(m, n)\, x_c(i + m,\, j + n).
\]
(Deep learning libraries call this convolution even though it’s really correlation, since the mask isn’t flipped, and as the weights are learned anyway it makes no difference.) After the convolution comes a simple nonlinearity, nowadays almost always the ReLU, max(0, y), and every so often a pooling layer that shrinks the image, for example by keeping the maximum of each 2 × 2 block. Without the nonlinearity, a stack of convolutions would just be one big convolution, so the ReLU is what lets a deep network compute something more interesting than a linear filter.
Two properties make convolution layers a really good fit for images. They’re local, since each output only looks at a small neighbourhood, and they share weights, since the same mask is used at every position, so a feature detector that’s learned to find an eye in one corner of the image finds it everywhere else too. That makes the number of parameters tiny compared with a fully connected layer. A layer from 64 channels to 64 channels with 3 × 3 masks has 64 · 64 · 9 + 64 = 36,928 parameters, no matter how big the image is, while a fully connected layer between two 64-channel images of size 56 × 56 would need about 4 × 1010. As layers are stacked and the image is pooled down, each unit sees a bigger and bigger part of the original picture, and the learned filters go from edge and colour detectors in the first layer (they look a lot like the Gabor-like and centre-surround masks of Section 3.3.2) to parts of objects and then whole objects deeper in, which is something people have checked by visualizing what makes each unit respond.
The size of the output is a little formula that’s worth knowing. With input width W, mask size k, zero padding P on each side and stride S (how far the mask jumps between positions), the output width is
\[
W_{\text{out}} = \Big\lfloor \frac{W - k + 2P}{S} \Big\rfloor + 1 ,
\]
so a 3 × 3 mask with padding 1 and stride 1 keeps the size the same, which is the most common choice.

Loops over output channels and mask entries are fine, but try to let NumPy handle the image positions. The check compares one output channel with cv2.filter2D and counts the parameters of the layer.

4.1.3 Training
A network for classification ends with one number per class, called the logits s1, …, sK, which get turned into probabilities by the softmax,
\[
p_k = \frac{e^{s_k}}{\sum_j e^{s_j}} ,
\]
and if the correct class is y, the loss for this example is the cross-entropy L = −log py, which is zero when the network puts all its probability on the right answer and grows without bound when it’s confidently wrong. Training means adjusting all the weights to make the average loss over the training images small, and it’s done by gradient descent, w ← w − η ∂L/∂w, with some learning rate η, using small random batches of images at a time (that’s stochastic gradient descent).
The gradients are computed by the chain rule, applied backwards through the layers, which is called backpropagation, and the very first step of it, the gradient of the loss with respect to the logits, has a really clean form that’s worth deriving. Write the loss as \(L = -s_y + \log\sum_j e^{s_j}\) and differentiate,
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial s_k} = -[k = y] + \frac{e^{s_k}}{\sum_j e^{s_j}} = p_k - [k = y],
\]
so the gradient is just the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot vector of the correct answer. If the network gives the right class probability 0.7, the gradient pushes that logit up by 0.3 and pushes every other logit down by its own probability. Everything else in backpropagation is the same kind of bookkeeping, layer by layer, and libraries like PyTorch do it automatically.
Here’s the whole process in NumPy, on a toy problem, where we train a small network to tell apart 8 × 8 images of horizontal bars, vertical bars and diagonal bars with noise added. The network has one hidden layer of 32 ReLU units, which is a fully connected network rather than a convolutional one, but the training loop is exactly the same idea.

def bar_images(n, rng):
    X = np.zeros((n, 8, 8)); y = rng.integers(0, 3, n)
    for i in range(n):
        k = rng.integers(1, 7)
        if y[i] == 0: X[i, k, :] = 1
        elif y[i] == 1: X[i, :, k] = 1
        else: X[i] = np.eye(8, k=k - 3)
    return (X + rng.normal(0, 0.5, X.shape)).reshape(n, 64), y

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xtr, ytr = bar_images(3000, rng); Xte, yte = bar_images(500, rng)
W1 = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (64, 32)); b1 = np.zeros(32); W2 = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (32, 3)); b2 = np.zeros(3)
losses, accs = [], []
for step in range(600):
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(Xtr), 64)
    X, y = Xtr[idx], ytr[idx]
    h = np.maximum(0, X @ W1 + b1)                      # forward pass
    s = h @ W2 + b2
    p = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True)); p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    losses.append(-np.log(p[np.arange(64), y]).mean())
    ds = p.copy(); ds[np.arange(64), y] -= 1; ds /= 64   # softmax cross-entropy gradient: p - onehot
    dW2, db2 = h.T @ ds, ds.sum(0)                       # backward pass, by the chain rule
    dh = ds @ W2.T; dh[h <= 0] = 0
    dW1, db1 = X.T @ dh, dh.sum(0)
    for P, dP in [(W1, dW1), (b1, db1), (W2, dW2), (b2, db2)]:
        P -= 0.1 * dP
    if step % 20 == 0:
        accs.append((step, np.mean(np.argmax(np.maximum(0, Xte @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2, 1) == yte)))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2)); ax2 = ax.twinx()
ax.plot(losses, color="#3B6FB6", lw=0.8, label="training loss")
ax2.plot(*zip(*accs), color="#E07A3F", label="test accuracy")
ax.set_xlabel("step"); ax.set_ylabel("loss"); ax2.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax2.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
fig.legend(loc="center right", fontsize=8); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("final test accuracy:", accs[-1][1])




Training loss (blue) and accuracy on held-out images (orange) for a small network learning to tell three kinds of noisy bar images apart, trained with stochastic gradient descent in NumPy.




final test accuracy: 0.936


The same thing in PyTorch, for a real convolutional network on real images, looks like this (it isn’t run here, since the browser can’t load PyTorch, but it runs as it is on your own computer with torchvision installed):
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torchvision
net = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
    nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
    nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 * 8 * 8, 10))
data = torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(".", train=True, download=True,
                                    transform=torchvision.transforms.ToTensor())
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(data, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)
opt = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=0.05, momentum=0.9)
for epoch in range(5):
    for images, labels in loader:
        loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(images), labels)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()     # backward() is backpropagation
In practice almost nobody trains a vision network from scratch for a new problem. The standard move is transfer learning: take a network that was trained on ImageNet, keep all its layers except the last one, and retrain only that last layer (or fine-tune everything with a small learning rate) on your own, much smaller dataset. The early layers learned general features like edges and textures that are useful for almost any picture, so a few hundred labelled images can be enough, which is how most of the course projects end up working.

Subtract the largest logit in each row before exponentiating, since e1000 overflows but the softmax doesn’t change when you shift all the logits by the same amount. The check compares your gradient with finite differences and tries some huge logits.

    """Average softmax cross-entropy of logits s (n, K) for labels y, and its gradient (n, K)."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    s = rng.normal(size=(5, 4)); y = rng.integers(0, 4, 5)
    L, g = softmax_xent(s, y)
    num = np.zeros_like(s); eps = 1e-6
    for i in range(5):
        for k in range(4):
            sp = s.copy(); sp[i, k] += eps; sm = s.copy(); sm[i, k] -= eps
            num[i, k] = (softmax_xent(sp, y)[0] - softmax_xent(sm, y)[0]) / (2 * eps)
    big, _ = softmax_xent(np.array([[1000.0, 0.0, -1000.0]]), np.array([0]))
    print(f"loss {L:.4f}, largest gradient error {np.abs(g - num).max():.1e}, loss on huge logits {big}")
    return np.abs(g - num).max() < 1e-6 and np.isfinite(big) and abs(big) < 1e-9

text:
4.2 Faces

4.2.1 Detection, verification and identification
Faces get two whole lectures, and there’s a good reason, since face recognition is probably the most widely deployed (and most argued about) application of computer vision. It helps to separate three tasks that often get lumped together. Detection finds the faces in a picture, which is what Chapter 1 did with skin colour and templates, and which modern detectors do with a network that outputs boxes. Verification asks whether two face images show the same person, a yes or no question, which is what unlocking a phone does. Identification asks who a face is, by comparing it against a gallery of known people, which is what a search through a database of photos does.
The way modern systems do both verification and identification is through embeddings. A network maps each aligned face crop to a vector, often 512 numbers long and normalized to unit length, and it’s trained so that two photos of the same person map to nearby vectors while photos of different people end up far apart. Comparing faces then just means comparing vectors, usually by cosine similarity, which for unit vectors is the dot product, and that’s nice because the network never needs to have seen the people it’s comparing. Training uses huge collections of face photos labelled by identity, and a lot of the research in this area has been about the loss function, from triplet losses (pull an anchor towards a photo of the same person and push it away from a photo of somebody else, as in Google’s FaceNet) to losses like ArcFace that add an angular margin to the softmax of Section 4.1.3 so the classes are forced further apart.
The lecture’s reading list is also a tour of the datasets that drove the field, and they’re worth knowing because each one was made to expose a weakness of the methods before it. Labeled Faces in the Wild (LFW, 2007) has about 13,000 photos of 5,749 people collected from news sites, and it was the standard verification benchmark until methods passed 99% on it. MegaFace (2016) tested identification against a million distractors, FaceScrub provided clean photos of celebrities, IARPA Janus Benchmark A (IJB-A, 2015) brought in much harder poses and image quality, CFP (Celebrities in Frontal-Profile, 2016) paired frontal with profile views, and AFLW2000 is used for aligning faces at large poses. VGGFace2 (Cao and colleagues, 2018) collected millions of images with lots of variation in pose and age for training.


4.2.2 Measuring a verifier
A verifier compares the similarity score of two faces with a threshold, and there are two ways for it to be wrong. It can reject a genuine pair (a false non-match, which is annoying) or accept an impostor pair (a false match, which is a security problem). Moving the threshold trades one for the other, and the honest way to describe a verifier is to show the whole trade-off. If we compute scores for many genuine pairs and many impostor pairs, then for each threshold τ we get a false match rate FMR(τ), the fraction of impostor scores at or above τ, and a false non-match rate FNMR(τ), the fraction of genuine scores below it. Plotting the true match rate 1 − FNMR against FMR as τ varies gives the ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic), which Fawcett’s tutorial in the reading list covers carefully. Two summary numbers are common. The equal error rate is where FMR = FNMR, and systems for security are usually quoted as a true match rate at a fixed, very small false match rate, like 10−4, since that’s the regime where they’re used.

Exercise 4.2.1 (Error rates of a face verifier) Write error_rates(genuine, impostor, thresholds), which returns two arrays, the false match rate (fraction of impostor scores ≥ τ) and false non-match rate (fraction of genuine scores < τ) at each threshold, and equal_error_rate(genuine, impostor), which returns the error rate at the threshold where the two are closest, trying every score as a threshold. The check uses synthetic similarity scores and plots the ROC curve.

def equal_error_rate(genuine, impostor):

def test():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    gen = np.clip(rng.normal(0.62, 0.12, 4000), -1, 1); imp = np.clip(rng.normal(0.1, 0.12, 20000), -1, 1)
    th = np.linspace(-0.2, 1.0, 241)
    fmr, fnmr = (np.asarray(a, float) for a in error_rates(gen, imp, th))
    eer = float(equal_error_rate(gen, imp))
    from math import erf, sqrt
    theory = 0.5 * (1 - erf(0.26 / 0.12 / sqrt(2)))      # both errors at the midpoint 0.36
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.6, 3.3))
    ax.semilogx(np.maximum(fmr, 1e-5), 1 - fnmr); ax.set_xlabel("false match rate"); ax.set_ylabel("true match rate")
    fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    print(f"equal error rate {eer:.4f} (for these two Gaussians, theory says {theory:.4f})")

4.2.3 Pose and aging
The March 19 lecture picks up the two things that make face recognition hard even for good networks. The first is pose. A profile view shows a completely different set of pixels from a frontal view, and half the face is hidden, so matching a profile against a frontal photo is much harder than matching two frontal ones, which is what the CFP benchmark was built to measure. A common approach, which the papers by Zhu and colleagues in the reading list develop, is to fit a 3D face model to the photo, estimate the pose, and then either render the face from the front or align landmarks in 3D, which brings the image formation of Section 2.1.2 right back into a deep learning pipeline. The second is aging. Faces change over years, especially for children, and the question of how long a face photo stays useful for recognition was studied in a longitudinal analysis by Best-Rowden and Jain (2017), using repeated mugshots of the same people over many years, which found that genuine similarity scores drop slowly with the time between photos, and that for most people recognition stays reliable over several years but not indefinitely.


4.2.4 Facial expressions
Recognizing what a face is doing, rather than whose it is, has a nice classical solution in the reading list, the paper by Black and Yacoob (1997) on recognizing facial expressions from image motion. Their idea was to describe the motion of each part of the face with a small parametric model rather than a free flow field. The face as a whole moves roughly like a plane, and each eye, eyebrow and the mouth gets its own model with a few parameters, the simplest of which is the affine flow
\[
u(x, y) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 y, \qquad v(x, y) = a_3 + a_4 x + a_5 y ,
\]
with (x, y) measured from the centre of the region. Six numbers capture translation, rotation, scaling and shearing of the region, and Black and Yacoob added a curvature term for the mouth and eyebrows. The parameters are estimated robustly from the image derivatives, using the same brightness constancy constraint as Section 3.5.1 but with the flow replaced by the model, and then, for each frame, they’re turned into simple descriptions like “the mouth is stretching horizontally” or “the brows are rising”, and a smile or surprise is recognized from the sequence of these descriptions over time (onset, apex, offset). It’s a nice example of how a little bit of structure can make motion much easier to interpret than a raw flow field, and of the aperture problem disappearing, since six parameters for a whole region are very well determined even though each pixel’s flow isn’t.

The check generates the flow of a mouth region that stretches horizontally and opens a little, adds noise, and also reads off the horizontal stretch a1, which is the kind of number Black and Yacoob turned into “mouth stretching”.

    x = rng.uniform(-20, 20, 300); y = rng.uniform(-8, 8, 300)
    a = np.array([0.5, 0.06, 0.0, -0.2, 0.0, 0.03])
    u = a[0] + a[1] * x + a[2] * y + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 300); v = a[3] + a[4] * x + a[5] * y + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 300)

    return got.shape == (6,) and np.abs(got - a).max() < 0.02

4.2.5 Biometrics
Face recognition is one kind of biometric, a way of recognizing people from their bodies or behaviour, along with fingerprints, iris patterns, voice, gait and others. They all share the verification framework of Section 4.2.2, with genuine and impostor score distributions and a threshold, and they differ in how distinctive and how permanent the trait is and how easy it is to collect, which is where faces win, since a camera can capture them at a distance without anyone’s cooperation. That same convenience is what makes face recognition so contested. It can be used for surveillance that people never agreed to, and evaluations like NIST’s Face Recognition Vendor Test have measured that many algorithms have different error rates for different demographic groups, which matters a lot when a false match can mean a wrongful arrest. We’ll come back to this in Section 5.8, and it’s worth keeping in mind while working through the methods, since the error rates in an ROC curve turn into real people’s experiences once a system is deployed.

4.3 Stereo And Multiple Views
In Section 2.4 the two cameras were side by side and pointing the same way, which made matches lie on the same row. Real camera pairs aren’t arranged that neatly, and in structure from motion the “second camera” is just the same camera a moment later, somewhere else, pointing somewhere else. This section is about the geometry that ties two arbitrary views together, which is beautiful and surprisingly compact.

4.3.1 Epipolar geometry
Take two pinhole cameras with centres O1 and O2 and a scene point P. The three points O1, O2 and P span a plane, the epipolar plane, and the image of P in each camera has to lie where that plane cuts the image, which is a line, the epipolar line. So if we know where P appears in the first image, its match in the second image has to lie on a known line, and the search for correspondences is one-dimensional again, just along a slanted line instead of a row. All the epipolar lines in one image pass through one point, the epipole, which is the image of the other camera’s centre.
To turn this into algebra, work in the first camera’s coordinates, and let the second camera be rotated by R and translated by t, so a point P1 in the first camera’s coordinates is P2 = R P1 + t in the second camera’s. Let x1 and x2 be the image points as homogeneous 3-vectors in normalized coordinates (that is, after removing the intrinsics, x = K−1(u, v, 1)⊤), so P1 = Z1x1 and P2 = Z2x2 for the unknown depths. The three vectors t, Rx1 and x2, all seen in the second camera’s frame, lie in the epipolar plane, so the triple product is zero,
\[
x_2^\top\big(t \times R\,x_1\big) = 0 .
\]
Writing the cross product with t as multiplication by the skew-symmetric matrix [t]×, this becomes
\[
x_2^\top E\, x_1 = 0, \qquad E = [t]_\times R, \qquad [t]_\times = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -t_3 & t_2 \\ t_3 & 0 & -t_1 \\ -t_2 & t_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} .
\]
E is the essential matrix (Longuet-Higgins, 1981), and it packs the whole relative pose of the two cameras into nine numbers, defined up to scale. Since [t]× has rank 2, so does E, and for a point x1 in the first image, the vector E x1 is exactly the epipolar line in the second image in the homogeneous line notation of Section 2.2.2. If we work in pixel coordinates instead, the same constraint holds with the fundamental matrix F = K2−⊤ E K1−1,
\[
\tilde{x}_2^\top F\, \tilde{x}_1 = 0 ,
\]
where x̃ are homogeneous pixel coordinates. F also has rank 2 and is defined up to scale, so it has 7 degrees of freedom, and the great thing about it is that it can be estimated from point matches alone, without knowing anything about the cameras.


4.3.2 The eight-point algorithm
Each match (x̃1, x̃2) gives one equation x̃2⊤ F x̃1 = 0, and this equation is linear in the nine entries of F. Writing out the product, with x̃1 = (u1, v1, 1) and x̃2 = (u2, v2, 1), it’s
\[
\big(u_2 u_1,\; u_2 v_1,\; u_2,\; v_2 u_1,\; v_2 v_1,\; v_2,\; u_1,\; v_1,\; 1\big) \cdot f = 0 ,
\]
where f lists the entries of F row by row. Eight matches give eight such rows, which (with F only defined up to scale) is enough to pin it down, and with more matches we solve the least squares problem with ‖f‖ = 1 by taking the right singular vector with the smallest singular value, exactly as for the vanishing point in Section 2.2.2. The estimate won’t quite have rank 2 because of noise, so the last step forces it, by taking the SVD of F, setting the smallest singular value to zero and multiplying back.
There’s one more step that matters a lot in practice, which Hartley pointed out in a 1997 paper with the memorable title “In defense of the eight-point algorithm”. Pixel coordinates are numbers in the hundreds, so the entries of each row range from about 1 to about 105, and that makes the least squares problem badly conditioned. The fix is to normalize first. Translate each image’s points so their centroid is at the origin and scale them so their average distance from it is √2, run the algorithm on the normalized points, and undo the normalization at the end. If T1 and T2 are the normalizing transforms (3 × 3 matrices acting on homogeneous points) and F̂ is the matrix found for the normalized points, then F = T2⊤ F̂ T1. This small change makes the results dramatically more accurate, and it’s a good example of how much numerical care matters in geometry.

Exercise 4.3.1 (The normalized eight-point algorithm) Write eight_point(p1, p2), which takes matching pixel coordinates of shape (n, 2) in two images, with n ≥ 8, and returns the fundamental matrix F, scaled to unit norm, using Hartley’s normalization and the rank-2 step. The check builds two synthetic cameras looking at random points, adds half a pixel of noise to the matches, and measures the average distance of each point in the second image from its epipolar line.

    """Normalized eight-point estimate of F (3 x 3, unit norm) from matches p1, p2 (n, 2)."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError

# [Setup] Two cameras looking at the same random 3D points; p1 and p2 are the matched pixel coordinates.
_rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
K_cam = np.array([[700.0, 0, 320], [0, 700, 240], [0, 0, 1]])
R_rel, _ = cv2.Rodrigues(np.array([0.05, -0.25, 0.03])); t_rel = np.array([-1.0, 0.1, 0.15])
P3 = np.c_[_rng.uniform(-2, 2, 60), _rng.uniform(-1.5, 1.5, 60), _rng.uniform(5, 9, 60)]
def _px(P):
    h = P @ K_cam.T
    return h[:, :2] / h[:, 2:]
p1_true, p2_true = _px(P3), _px(P3 @ R_rel.T + t_rel)
p1 = p1_true + _rng.normal(0, 0.5, p1_true.shape); p2 = p2_true + _rng.normal(0, 0.5, p2_true.shape)



def test():
    F = np.asarray(eight_point(p1, p2), float)
    h1 = np.c_[p1_true, np.ones(60)]; h2 = np.c_[p2_true, np.ones(60)]
    lines = h1 @ F.T
    dist = np.abs(np.sum(lines * h2, 1)) / np.linalg.norm(lines[:, :2], axis=1)
    sv = np.linalg.svd(F, compute_uv=False)
    print(f"mean distance from epipolar lines {dist.mean():.3f} px;  singular values {np.round(sv / sv[0], 6)}")
    return F.shape == (3, 3) and abs(np.linalg.norm(F) - 1) < 1e-9 and sv[2] / sv[0] < 1e-10 and dist.mean() < 1.0

4.3.3 Triangulation
Once we know the two camera matrices P1 = K1[I | 0] and P2 = K2[R | t] and a match, getting the 3D point back is called triangulation. In a perfect world the two rays through the matched pixels meet at P, but with noise they miss each other slightly, so again we solve a small least squares problem. For each camera, the projection says that the homogeneous image point x̃ is parallel to PiX, where X is the homogeneous 3D point, so x̃ × (PiX) = 0. Two of the three components of this cross product are independent, and writing pik⊤ for the k-th row of Pi, they’re
\[
u\,(p^{3\top} X) - p^{1\top} X = 0, \qquad v\,(p^{3\top} X) - p^{2\top} X = 0 .
\]
Two cameras give four equations in the four entries of X, which is again a homogeneous least squares problem solved with the SVD, and then we divide by the last entry. This is the linear or DLT method, and it’s what cv2.triangulatePoints does. It doesn’t minimize the actual pixel errors, so more careful methods refine it, but it’s a very good start. And it’s the general version of the depth formula Z = fB/d from Section 2.4.1, which you can check by plugging in the side-by-side cameras.

The check triangulates the noise-free matches of the synthetic cameras and compares with cv2.triangulatePoints.

    got = np.array([triangulate(P1, P2, p1_true[i], p2_true[i]) for i in range(10)], float)
    ref = cv2.triangulatePoints(P1, P2, p1_true[:10].T, p2_true[:10].T); ref = (ref[:3] / ref[3]).T
    print("largest error against the true points:", np.abs(got - P3[:10]).max())

4.3.4 Rectification and multiview stereo
Searching along slanted epipolar lines is awkward, so stereo systems usually rectify the images first, warping each one with a homography (a 3 × 3 matrix acting on homogeneous pixel coordinates) so that the epipolar lines become horizontal rows, and the side-by-side geometry of Section 2.4 applies, including block matching along rows and Z = fB/d. OpenCV does this with cv2.stereoRectify once the cameras are calibrated. With more than two cameras, multiview stereo combines the evidence from all of them, for example by testing, for each pixel of a reference image, a range of depths and checking how consistent the colours are in all the other views at the projected positions (the plane-sweep idea), and the best systems now produce dense 3D models of whole buildings from collections of photos.


4.3.5 Active stereo and structured light
Stereo matching fails on blank surfaces because there’s nothing to match, so an obvious trick is to put the texture there ourselves. Active stereo replaces one of the cameras with a projector, or adds a projector to a stereo pair, and shines a known pattern onto the scene. The projector is geometrically just a camera running backwards, so the triangulation of Section 4.3.3 works unchanged, as long as we know which projector pixel lit each camera pixel. The simplest version sweeps a single laser stripe across the object, so each image has one bright curve whose position along each row gives depth, which is how a lot of industrial 3D scanners work. Faster systems project a sequence of binary stripe patterns, so that the on/off sequence a camera pixel sees over, say, 10 patterns spells out the projector column in binary (210 = 1024 columns from 10 images). The patterns are usually Gray codes, an ordering of binary numbers in which consecutive numbers differ in only one bit, so a pixel right at the boundary between two stripes can only be off by one column instead of being completely wrong. The first Kinect (2010) used a single fixed pattern of infrared speckles, matched against a stored reference image, which let it measure depth at video rate.

Exercise 4.3.3 (Gray codes) The Gray code of a number n is n XOR (n >> 1). Write gray_encode(n) and gray_decode(g), where decoding uses the fact that the binary number’s bits are the running XOR of the Gray code’s bits from the top down, which you can compute by repeatedly XOR-ing g with itself shifted right. Both should work on NumPy integer arrays. The check confirms that consecutive codes differ in exactly one bit and that decoding undoes encoding for all 10-bit columns.

4.3.6 Structure from motion
Now suppose we have just one camera, moving through a static scene, and we track some points through many frames with something like the Lucas-Kanade tracker of Section 3.5.4. Can we get back both the 3D shape of the scene and the motion of the camera? That’s structure from motion, and under the weak perspective model of Section 2.1.3 there’s a lovely answer, the factorization method of Tomasi and Kanade (1992).
Under orthographic projection (weak perspective with the scale folded in), the image of point j in frame i is uij = mi · Sj + ai and vij = ni · Sj + bi, where Sj is the 3D point, mi and ni are the first two rows of the camera’s rotation in frame i, and (ai, bi) is a translation. If we measure every point relative to the centroid of all points in each frame, the translations drop out (as long as we put the world origin at the centroid of the 3D points). Now stack all the measurements of F frames and P points into one big 2F × P measurement matrix W, with the u’s of frame i in row i and the v’s in row F + i. Then
\[
W = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} m_1^\top \\ \vdots \\ m_F^\top \\ n_1^\top \\ \vdots \\ n_F^\top \end{pmatrix}}_{M\ (2F \times 3)} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} S_1 & \cdots & S_P \end{pmatrix}}_{S\ (3 \times P)} ,
\]
so W, however big, has rank at most 3. That’s the whole insight. Take the SVD of W, keep the three largest singular values, W ≈ U3Σ3V3⊤, and set M̂ = U3Σ31/2 and Ŝ = Σ31/2V3⊤. This recovers motion and shape, but only up to an unknown invertible 3 × 3 matrix A, since M̂A and A−1Ŝ multiply to the same W. To pin A down Tomasi and Kanade use the fact that each mi and ni must be unit vectors and perpendicular to each other, which gives linear equations for the symmetric matrix AA⊤, and then A follows from a Cholesky factorization (up to a rotation of the whole scene, which really can’t be recovered, since you can’t tell the world’s orientation from images alone). The truncated SVD also gives the best rank-3 fit to noisy data, so noise is averaged over all frames and points at once.
For perspective cameras, the modern approach is incremental. Estimate the relative pose of two views from the essential matrix of Section 4.3.1, triangulate points, add more views one at a time, and then refine everything together with bundle adjustment, a big nonlinear least squares problem over all camera poses and 3D points that minimizes the total reprojection error. That’s how systems like COLMAP build 3D models from thousands of tourist photos.

Exercise 4.3.4 (Factorization) Write factorize(W), which takes a 2F × P measurement matrix, subtracts each row’s mean, and returns the rank-3 factors M̂ (2F × 3) and Ŝ (3 × P) from the SVD as above, without the metric upgrade. The check builds an orthographic sequence of a random point cloud seen by a rotating camera, adds noise, confirms that M̂Ŝ reproduces the centred data to within the noise, and that the shape is correct up to an invertible linear map.


def factorize(W):
    """Tomasi-Kanade affine factorization of a 2F x P measurement matrix. Returns (M, S)."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError


def test():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
    S = rng.normal(size=(3, 40)); S -= S.mean(1, keepdims=True)
    us, vs = [], []
    for i in range(12):
        R, _ = cv2.Rodrigues(np.array([0.1 * i, 0.3 * np.sin(i / 3), 0.05 * i]))
        us.append(R[0] @ S + 3.0); vs.append(R[1] @ S - 1.0)
    W = np.vstack(us + vs) + rng.normal(0, 0.01, (24, 40))
    M, Sh = (np.asarray(a, float) for a in factorize(W))
    Wc = W - W.mean(1, keepdims=True)
    resid = np.abs(M @ Sh - Wc).max()
    A = np.linalg.lstsq(Sh.T, S.T, rcond=None)[0]       # best linear map from recovered to true shape
    shape_err = np.abs(Sh.T @ A - S.T).max()
    print(f"largest residual {resid:.4f};  shape error after the best linear map {shape_err:.4f}")
    return M.shape == (24, 3) and Sh.shape == (3, 40) and resid < 0.05 and shape_err < 0.05

title: 4  Deep Learning, Faces and Multiple Views
text:
4.4 Segmentation With Deep Networks
The last lecture in this block comes back to segmentation, which in Chapter 1 meant thresholding and connected components, and asks what deep networks do with it. There are a few flavours. Semantic segmentation labels every pixel with a class (road, car, person, sky), instance segmentation also separates individual objects (this car versus that car), and medical image segmentation, which the course returns to often, usually means outlining one organ or tumour precisely.
The first big step was the fully convolutional network of Long, Shelhamer and Darrell (2015), who noticed that a classification network with its final fully connected layers replaced by convolutions produces a coarse map of class scores rather than one score per image, and that this map can be upsampled back to the original resolution and trained pixel by pixel with the cross-entropy loss of Section 4.1.3. The problem is that the pooling layers throw away fine detail, so boundaries come out blurry, and the fix that stuck was U-Net (Ronneberger, Fischer and Brox, 2015), designed for biomedical images. It has a contracting path that pools down, like a classifier, and an expanding path that upsamples back up, and at each resolution it copies the features from the contracting path across to the expanding path (the skip connections), so the decoder gets both the coarse “what” from deep layers and the precise “where” from shallow ones. U-Net works well with surprisingly few training images, which is why it’s still a default in medical imaging. For instance segmentation, Mask R-CNN (He and colleagues, 2017) adds a small mask-predicting branch to an object detector, and more recently, models like Meta’s Segment Anything (2023) were trained on a billion masks and can segment almost any object from a click or a box.
To measure how good a segmentation is, we compare the predicted mask A with the ground-truth mask B. The two standard scores are the intersection over union (or Jaccard index) and the Dice coefficient,
\[
\text{IoU} = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}, \qquad \text{Dice} = \frac{2|A\cap B|}{|A| + |B|} .
\]
They’re closely related. Using |A| + |B| = |A ∪ B| + |A ∩ B| and dividing top and bottom by |A ∪ B|, Dice = 2 IoU/(1 + IoU), so they always rank segmentations the same way, but Dice is always the larger of the two (except at 0 and 1), which is worth remembering when comparing numbers across papers that use different ones. Both ignore true negatives, which is the right thing to do when the object is small compared with the background, since a method that labels everything as background would otherwise look very accurate.

5.1 Generative Models
The last part of the course covers a lot of ground, one or two lectures per topic (CS 585 schedule). There’s a lecture on generative models, GANs and diffusion, then one on how light reflects off surfaces and how to get shape back from shading, one on supervised, semi-supervised and unsupervised learning, one on image registration with absolute orientation, quaternions and the iterative closest point algorithm, one on transformers, one on vision-and-language navigation, and a final one on tracking many objects with many cameras and on computer vision and ethics. The chapter follows the same order. Some of these topics could fill a course on their own, so the aim here is to get the core idea of each one straight, with a derivation where there’s a clean one and a small computation to make it concrete.
Everything in the previous chapters went from images to some description, a label, a box, a depth, a flow field. Generative models go the other way and produce images, and the goal is usually stated in terms of probability. There’s some unknown distribution pdata over images (photos of faces, say), we have samples from it, and we want a model we can draw new samples from that look like they came from the same distribution. The two families the lecture covers attack this in very different ways.

text:
5.1.1 Generative adversarial networks
The GAN idea (Goodfellow and colleagues, 2014) is to train two networks against each other. A generator G takes random noise z, usually a vector of Gaussian numbers, and turns it into an image G(z), and a discriminator D takes an image and outputs the probability that it’s real rather than generated. The discriminator is trained to tell real from fake, and the generator is trained to fool it, which written as one objective is the game
\[
\min_G \max_D \; V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{z}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(z))\big)\big].
\]
It’s worth seeing what this game actually optimizes, because the answer is pretty elegant. Let pg be the distribution of the generated images. For a fixed generator, the value is ∫ [pdata(x) log D(x) + pg(x) log(1 − D(x))] dx, and we can maximize the integrand separately at each x. The function a log D + b log(1 − D) has its maximum at D = a/(a + b), so the best discriminator is
\[
D^*(x) = \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_{\text{data}}(x) + p_g(x)} ,
\]
which makes sense, since it says “real” in proportion to how much more likely x is under the data. Plugging it back in and writing m = (pdata + pg)/2 for the mixture,
\[
V(D^*, G) = \int p_{\text{data}}\log\frac{p_{\text{data}}}{2m} + \int p_g \log\frac{p_g}{2m} = -\log 4 + 2\,\mathrm{JS}(p_{\text{data}}\,\|\,p_g),
\]
where JS is the Jensen-Shannon divergence, the average of the Kullback-Leibler divergences of the two distributions from their mixture. The JS divergence is never negative and is zero only when the distributions are equal, so with a perfect discriminator the generator’s job is exactly to make pg equal pdata, and at that point D* = 1/2 everywhere, since the discriminator can’t do better than guessing.
In practice the two networks are trained by alternating gradient steps, and that’s where the trouble is. The game can oscillate instead of converging, and the generator can find a few images that fool the discriminator and produce only those, which is called mode collapse. A lot of work went into stabilizing GANs, and by around 2019 networks like StyleGAN were producing faces that people couldn’t tell from photos, which is also when “deepfakes” became a public concern (more on that in Section 5.8).

The check confirms that V(D*) = −log 4 + 2 JS(p‖q) for random distributions and that no other discriminator does better.

5.1.2 Diffusion models
Diffusion models, which took over image generation around 2021 and are behind systems like Stable Diffusion and DALL·E 2, work in a completely different way, and their training is much more stable. The idea (Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues in 2015, made practical by Ho, Jain and Abbeel’s DDPM paper in 2020) is to take an image and destroy it slowly by adding a little Gaussian noise at each of T steps, until after maybe a thousand steps it’s pure noise, and then to train a network to undo one step at a time. Generating a new image then means starting from pure noise and running the learned undoing T times.
The forward, noising process is fixed, with no learning in it at all. With a schedule of small variances β1, …, βT,
\[
x_t = \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\; x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\;\varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I).
\]
The √(1 − βt) factor shrinks the image a bit at each step so that the total variance stays bounded. The really useful fact is that we can jump straight to any step t without simulating the ones in between. Write αt = 1 − βt and ᾱt = α1α2⋯αt. If xt−1 = √ᾱt−1 x0 + (Gaussian noise with variance 1 − ᾱt−1), then xt = √αt xt−1 + √βt εt has the mean √(αtᾱt−1) x0 = √ᾱt x0 and, since independent Gaussian variances add, noise variance αt(1 − ᾱt−1) + βt = 1 − αtᾱt−1 = 1 − ᾱt. So by induction
\[
x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\; x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\;\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I),
\]
which is a blend of the clean image and pure noise, with the image’s weight √ᾱt falling from about 1 to about 0 as t goes from 0 to T.
That formula makes training really simple. Take a training image x0, pick a random t and random noise ε, form xt with the formula, and train a network εθ(xt, t) to predict the noise that was added, with the plain squared error ‖ε − εθ(xt, t)‖² as the loss. (Ho and colleagues derived this from a variational bound on the likelihood and found that this simplified version works best.) The network is usually a U-Net, the same architecture as in Section 4.4, which makes sense, since predicting a noise image from a noisy image is an image-to-image task. To generate, start from xT ~ N(0, I) and step backwards, at each step using the predicted noise to estimate a slightly cleaner image and adding back a little fresh noise. Text-to-image systems also feed a text embedding into the network, so it learns to denoise towards images that match the description.

text:
5.2 Light And Surfaces
Back to physics for a bit. Chapter 2 explained where a scene point shows up in the image, and this section is about how bright it is, which depends on the light, on the direction the surface is facing and on what the surface is made of. Turning that around gives some classic ways of recovering shape from brightness, which is what the April 4 lecture covers, following Horn’s Robot Vision (Chapters 10 and 11).

5.2.1 Reflectance and the Lambertian model
How a surface reflects light is described by its bidirectional reflectance distribution function, or BRDF, which says, for light arriving from one direction, how much of it leaves in each other direction. A mirror sends everything into one direction, a shiny plastic has a bright highlight around the mirror direction, and a matte surface like chalk or paper scatters light evenly in all directions. That last case is the Lambertian surface, named after Johann Heinrich Lambert, who described it in 1760, and it looks equally bright from every viewing direction. Its brightness depends only on how squarely it faces the light. If the unit surface normal is n, the unit direction towards a distant light source is s, the light’s strength is folded into s and the surface’s albedo (the fraction of light it reflects) is ρ, then
\[
I = \rho\, \max(0,\; n \cdot s) ,
\]
which is Lambert’s cosine law, since n · s is the cosine of the angle between the normal and the light. The cosine comes from simple geometry: a beam of light of fixed width hitting a surface at a slant spreads over a bigger area, so each bit of surface gets less light.
If the surface is the graph of a depth function z(x, y), its slope at each point is described by the gradient (p, q) = (∂z/∂x, ∂z/∂y), and the normal is proportional to (−p, −q, 1). So for a given light, the brightness is a function of p and q alone,
\[
R(p, q) = \rho\,\frac{-p\,s_x - q\,s_y + s_z}{\sqrt{1 + p^2 + q^2}} ,
\]
which Horn calls the reflectance map. Drawn as contours in the (p, q) plane (gradient space), it shows which slopes give which brightness, and the important thing to notice is that one brightness value corresponds to a whole curve of possible slopes, so a single pixel’s brightness doesn’t determine the surface orientation. That’s one equation for two unknowns again, just like the aperture problem in Section 3.5.2.


5.2.2 Photometric stereo
The fix, which Woodham proposed in 1980, is to take several pictures of the same object from the same viewpoint, each lit by a different light. Each picture gives one equation per pixel, and with three or more lights we can solve for the orientation. For a Lambertian surface (and ignoring shadows) this is even linear. Let g = ρn, which packs the albedo and the normal into one vector, and stack the light directions s1, …, sk as the rows of a k × 3 matrix S. Then the k brightness values at a pixel are
\[
\begin{pmatrix} I_1 \\ \vdots \\ I_k \end{pmatrix} = S\, g ,
\]
so g is the least squares solution of a tiny linear system, the albedo is ρ = ‖g‖ and the normal is n = g/ρ. With exactly three lights in general position, S is invertible and g = S−1I. Once we have the normals, we can integrate the slopes p = −nx/nz and q = −ny/nz to get the depth, up to a constant. Photometric stereo is very accurate for the fine detail of a surface, and it’s used in industrial inspection and for capturing detailed faces for film.

Pixels where the albedo comes out zero should get a zero normal. The check renders a Lambertian sphere with a painted stripe under four lights and compares your normals with the true ones.

The check only looks at pixels lit by all four lights. Where a light doesn’t reach, the max(0, ·) in Lambert’s law kicks in, the equations stop being linear and the simple solve gives wrong answers, so real systems detect shadowed measurements and drop them, which is one reason to use more than three lights.


5.2.3 Shape from shading
With only one image, we’re back to one equation per pixel, R(p, q) = I(x, y), and two unknowns. Shape from shading makes up the difference with the extra assumption that the surface is smooth, a bit like Horn and Schunck did for optical flow, and Horn’s early work in the 1970s set the problem up as a partial differential equation solved outward from points where the orientation is known, like the bright spot where the surface faces the light directly, or along the object’s silhouette, where the normal is perpendicular to the viewing direction. It works on clean synthetic images, but real images break the assumptions (unknown albedo changes, unknown lights, shadows and highlights), and there’s also an ambiguity humans fall for too, since a bump lit from above looks exactly like a dent lit from below, which is why our brains assume the light comes from above. Shape from shading is mostly of historical interest now as a method, but the idea of using shading as a cue to shape is alive and well inside networks that estimate depth and normals from a single image.

text:
5.3 Learning With And Without Labels
The April 9 lecture steps back to look at the different kinds of machine learning used in vision. Supervised learning, where every training image comes with the right answer, is what Section 4.1.3 did, and it works very well but labels are expensive, especially for things like segmentation masks or medical images that need an expert. Unsupervised learning gets structure out of unlabelled data alone, and we’ve actually seen an example already, since the iterative threshold of Section 1.2.1 was k-means with k = 2. Semi-supervised learning sits in between, with a few labelled images and many unlabelled ones, and a simple, surprisingly effective method is self-training: train on the labelled images, use the model to label the unlabelled images it’s confident about (pseudo-labels), add those to the training set and repeat. Closely related is self-supervised learning, which makes up a training task whose labels come for free from the data, like predicting a hidden part of an image or recognizing that two augmented crops come from the same photo, and then reuses the learned features for the task we actually care about. Most large vision models today are pretrained that way.

5.3.1 Principal component analysis and eigenfaces
The classic unsupervised method in vision is principal component analysis, and the classic application is the eigenfaces of Turk and Pentland (1991), one of the first face recognition systems that really worked. Treat each aligned face image of N pixels as a vector in ℝN. Faces don’t fill that space at all, they lie close to a much lower-dimensional subspace, and PCA finds it. Subtract the mean face, stack the centred images as the rows of a matrix X, and take its SVD, X = UΣV⊤. The rows of V⊤ are the principal components, here images in their own right, the eigenfaces, and the first k of them span the k-dimensional subspace that captures as much of the variance in the data as possible. Each face is then described by just its k coordinates in that subspace, and recognition compares those coordinates.
There’s a neat exact statement of how good the approximation is. Projecting each centred image onto the first k components and reconstructing it leaves a total squared error equal to the sum of the squared singular values that were thrown away,
\[
\sum_i \big\|x_i - \hat{x}_i\big\|^2 = \sum_{j > k} \sigma_j^2 ,
\]
which follows from writing X in terms of its SVD and noticing that the reconstruction keeps exactly the first k terms of X = Σ σj uj vj⊤ (this is the Eckart-Young theorem, which says no rank-k approximation does better). It’s the same rank truncation as the factorization of Section 4.3.6, which is a nice example of one linear algebra fact doing very different jobs.

The check uses synthetic “faces” built from a few smooth patterns plus noise, and confirms the reconstruction error formula above.

text:
5.4 Registration

5.4.1 Aligning images
Registration means bringing two images, or two sets of points, into alignment, and it’s everywhere in medical imaging, which is where the April 11 lecture spends most of its time. A radiologist comparing a lung CT scan from this year with one from last year needs them aligned voxel by voxel before any change can be measured, and scans taken with different machines (CT and PET, say) need to be aligned before they can be overlaid. Every registration method has three ingredients: a family of transformations (rigid, affine, or a deformable warp, since lungs change shape as you breathe), a measure of how well two images match (SSD and normalized correlation from Chapter 1 work when the images have the same kind of contrast, and mutual information is used when they don’t, since it only asks that the intensities be predictable from each other) and an optimizer that searches for the transformation with the best score. When we can identify corresponding landmarks in the two images, the rigid case has an exact closed-form answer, which is the next topic.


5.4.2 Absolute orientation
Given points a1, …, an measured in one coordinate system and the same points b1, …, bn measured in another, find the rotation R and translation t that best map one onto the other, minimizing Σ‖bi − (R ai + t)‖². Photogrammetrists call this the absolute orientation problem, and Horn gave the classic closed-form solution in 1987 using quaternions, which is the “Horn” reading for this lecture.
The translation is the easy part. Setting the derivative with respect to t to zero gives t = b̄ − R ā, where the bars are centroids, so the best transformation maps one centroid onto the other, and after subtracting the centroids, ai’ = ai − ā and bi’ = bi − b̄, we only need the rotation. Expanding the square, ‖b’ − Ra’‖² = ‖b’‖² + ‖a’‖² − 2 b’·Ra’, since rotations don’t change lengths, so minimizing the error means maximizing Σ bi‘·R ai’.
Horn’s trick is to write the rotation as a unit quaternion q = (q0, qx, qy, qz), which represents the rotation by angle θ about the unit axis u as q = (cos(θ/2), sin(θ/2)u). The quantity we’re maximizing turns out to be a quadratic form in q, Σ b’·Ra’ = q⊤Nq, where N is a symmetric 4 × 4 matrix built from the nine sums Sxy = Σ a’xb’y and so on,
\[
N = \begin{pmatrix}
S_{xx}+S_{yy}+S_{zz} & S_{yz}-S_{zy} & S_{zx}-S_{xz} & S_{xy}-S_{yx} \\
S_{yz}-S_{zy} & S_{xx}-S_{yy}-S_{zz} & S_{xy}+S_{yx} & S_{zx}+S_{xz} \\
S_{zx}-S_{xz} & S_{xy}+S_{yx} & -S_{xx}+S_{yy}-S_{zz} & S_{yz}+S_{zy} \\
S_{xy}-S_{yx} & S_{zx}+S_{xz} & S_{yz}+S_{zy} & -S_{xx}-S_{yy}+S_{zz}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Maximizing q⊤Nq over unit vectors q is the eigenvalue problem yet again (the same Rayleigh quotient argument as for the axis of least second moment in Section 1.2.5), so the best rotation is the eigenvector of N with the largest eigenvalue, turned back into a rotation matrix with the standard formula
\[
R = \begin{pmatrix}
q_0^2+q_x^2-q_y^2-q_z^2 & 2(q_xq_y - q_0q_z) & 2(q_xq_z + q_0q_y)\\
2(q_yq_x + q_0q_z) & q_0^2-q_x^2+q_y^2-q_z^2 & 2(q_yq_z - q_0q_x)\\
2(q_zq_x - q_0q_y) & 2(q_zq_y + q_0q_x) & q_0^2-q_x^2-q_y^2+q_z^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
There’s an equivalent solution with the SVD of the 3 × 3 matrix of sums (Arun, Huang and Blostein, 1987, also known as the Kabsch algorithm), which needs a small fix to avoid returning a reflection, and Horn’s quaternion method has the nice property that it can never return a reflection, since every unit quaternion is a proper rotation. Quaternions are also how rotations are usually stored in robotics and graphics, since they don’t suffer from the gimbal lock of Euler angles and are easy to interpolate.

The check rotates and translates a random point cloud, adds noise, and compares with the true R and t, and also confirms that your R is a proper rotation.

5.4.3 The iterative closest point algorithm
Absolute orientation needs to know which point goes with which. Often we have two scans of the same surface, from a laser scanner or two CT scans, with no correspondences at all, just two clouds of points. The iterative closest point algorithm (Besl and McKay, 1992) handles this with an idea that’s simple to the point of being cheeky. Guess that each point of the moving cloud corresponds to its nearest point in the fixed cloud, solve the absolute orientation problem for those guessed pairs, move the cloud, and repeat. Each step can only lower the mean squared distance (the matching step lowers it for the current pose, and the alignment step lowers it for the current matches), so the algorithm converges, but only to a local minimum, so it needs a starting pose that’s roughly right. It’s the same alternating idea as k-means and the iterative threshold, which is a pattern that keeps turning up in this book. Real implementations add a spatial search structure so the nearest neighbours are fast, and throw away pairs that are too far apart to be real matches.


Setup: a reference alignment routine for the ICP demonstration
# [Setup] An SVD-based absolute orientation (Arun, Huang and Blostein), so ICP below runs whether or not Exercise 5.4.1 is done.
def kabsch(A, B):
    a0, b0 = A.mean(0), B.mean(0)
    U, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd((A - a0).T @ (B - b0))
    D = np.diag([1, 1, np.sign(np.linalg.det(Vt.T @ U.T))])
    R = Vt.T @ D @ U.T
    return R, b0 - R @ a0

Return the total R, t that map the original src onto dst, and the list of mean squared distances after each iteration. The check uses a noisy, twisted space curve rotated by about 20 degrees and confirms that the error decreases at every step. (A plain helix would be a bad test, by the way, since sliding a helix along its own axis while turning it maps it onto itself, so ICP can happily converge to the wrong pose.)

5.5 Transformers

5.5.1 Attention
Transformers came from machine translation (Vaswani and colleagues, “Attention is all you need”, 2017) and took over computer vision a few years later. Their central operation, attention, lets every element of a sequence look at every other element and decide how much to borrow from each. Each element, called a token, is a vector, and from it the network computes three vectors with learned linear maps, a query q, a key k and a value v. The output for token i is a weighted average of all the values, with weights given by how well token i’s query matches each key,
\[
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)\,V ,
\]
where the rows of Q, K and V are the queries, keys and values of the n tokens, d is their length, and the softmax is applied to each row, so each row of weights is positive and sums to one. Compare that with a convolution, which mixes each pixel only with a fixed neighbourhood using fixed weights. Attention mixes every token with every other one, with weights that depend on the content, which is much more flexible, at the price of n² work for n tokens.
The √d is there for a reason that’s worth spelling out. If the entries of a query and a key are independent with mean zero and variance one, their dot product is a sum of d such products, so it has variance d. For large d the logits would then be huge, the softmax would put almost all its weight on one token, and the gradients through it would vanish. Dividing by √d brings the variance back to one. A transformer layer runs several attention operations in parallel (multi-head attention, each head with its own maps, so different heads can attend to different things), followed by a small fully connected network applied to each token separately, with residual connections and normalization around both. Attention by itself doesn’t know the order of the tokens, since permuting the inputs just permutes the outputs, so position information is added to the tokens at the start, as positional encodings.


5.5.2 Vision transformers
The Vision Transformer, or ViT (Dosovitskiy and colleagues, 2021), applies this to images with almost no changes. Cut the image into a grid of patches, 16 × 16 pixels each, flatten each patch into a vector, map it linearly to the token length, add a positional encoding, and feed the sequence of patch tokens to a standard transformer, with an extra learned token whose final value is used for classification. A 224 × 224 image becomes 14 × 14 = 196 tokens. With little data, ViTs do worse than convolutional networks, since they don’t have the built-in assumptions that nearby pixels matter most and that features look the same everywhere, but trained on enough data they do better, and they’ve become the standard backbone for large vision and vision-language models.

The check confirms that the weights are rows of probabilities, that permuting the tokens permutes the outputs, and that a 224 × 224 RGB image gives 196 tokens of length 768.

5.6 Vision And Language
The April 18 lecture is on vision-and-language navigation, where an agent placed in a building has to follow an instruction like “walk past the kitchen, go up the stairs and stop by the second door on the left”. The standard benchmark is Room-to-Room (Anderson and colleagues, 2018), built on real 3D scans of houses from the Matterport3D dataset, in which the agent sees panoramic photos at each location and moves between viewpoints on a graph. It’s a really demanding combination, since the agent needs to ground words in what it sees (what does a kitchen look like, which way is “left” from here), keep track of where it is in the instruction, and plan, and success is measured by how often it ends up within a few metres of the goal.
What made this kind of task practical is models that put images and text in the same embedding space. CLIP (Radford and colleagues, 2021) trained an image encoder and a text encoder on 400 million image-caption pairs from the web with a contrastive loss, so that matching image and caption embeddings have high cosine similarity and non-matching ones low, the same embedding idea as the face verification of Section 4.2.1, with captions playing the role of identities. A model like that can score how well any view matches any phrase, which is just what a navigating agent needs, and more recent systems go further by connecting a vision encoder to a large language model that can reason about the instruction in words.

5.7 Many Cameras, Many Objects
The last technical lecture combines tracking from Chapter 3 with the multiview geometry of Chapter 4. With several cameras watching the same scene, like the thermal cameras Betke’s group used to reconstruct the 3D flight paths of bats emerging from caves, we have to solve the association problem twice, once over time, as in Section 3.2.1, and once across views, deciding which detection in camera 2 is the same object as a given detection in camera 1. The epipolar constraint of Section 4.3.1 gives the cost for the cross-view matching. A detection in camera 2 can only be the same object as a detection x1 in camera 1 if it lies on (or near) the epipolar line F x̃1, so the distance from that line is a natural cost, and the assignment methods of Section 3.2.1 do the rest. With three or more cameras the constraints get stronger, since a match has to be consistent in every pair, and once the matches are made, triangulation from Section 4.3.3 gives 3D positions, which can then be tracked over time with a 3D Kalman filter. The two association problems help each other, since tracking over time resolves ambiguities in a single frame (two bats might both lie near the same epipolar line in one frame but not in the next), and that’s what makes these systems work in very crowded scenes. When the objects move on a ground plane, as people do, a simpler alternative is to map each camera’s detections onto the ground with a homography, and associate them there by distance.

The check reuses the two cameras of Section 4.3.2 with the detections in camera 2 shuffled, and asks whether you recover the true pairing.

    return h[:, :2] / h[:, 2:]
view1 = _proj(objs) + _rng.normal(0, 0.5, (8, 2))

view2 = (_proj(objs @ R_c.T + t_c) + _rng.normal(0, 0.5, (8, 2)))[perm_c]

5.8 Computer Vision And Ethics
The course ends, rightly I think, with ethics, and it’s a good place for this book to end too, since a lot of the techniques we’ve worked through have direct consequences for people.
The most obvious issue is privacy and surveillance. Face recognition from Section 4.2, combined with the multi-camera tracking we just saw, makes it technically possible to follow people across a whole city without their knowledge, and different countries and cities have made very different choices about whether to allow that, with some American cities banning police use of face recognition and other places deploying it widely. The second is bias. Buolamwini and Gebru’s 2018 Gender Shades study showed that commercial gender classifiers were far less accurate for darker-skinned women than for lighter-skinned men, largely because of what was in the training data, and the NIST vendor tests mentioned in Section 4.2.5 found demographic differences in many face recognition algorithms. Those differences have consequences, as several wrongful arrests based on false face matches in the US have shown. The third is data and consent. Many of the big face datasets of Section 4.2.1 were built by scraping photos of people who never agreed to it, and some, like Microsoft’s MS-Celeb-1M, were withdrawn after criticism. The fourth is synthetic media. The generative models of Section 5.1 make convincing fake photos and videos cheap, which is a real problem for trust in images as evidence and for the people whose faces get used.
None of this means computer vision is a bad thing to work on. The same course started with the Camera Mouse, which lets people with severe paralysis use a computer by moving their head, and vision is behind medical image analysis, accessibility tools for blind people and a lot of science, including the bat and cell tracking that Betke’s group is known for. The point is that the choices made while building a system, which data to collect, which error rates to measure and for whom, where to set a threshold on an ROC curve, what to do when the system is unsure (remember the KidsRoom’s monsters, which just didn’t praise a child when unsure), are partly ethical choices, and the people best placed to make them well are the ones who understand how the methods work.
